But he held firm, a rock in the sea, a sea-rock that stands when the great crash comes, holding its own weight while the waves howl all around it; the cliffs and the foaming reefs roar in vain, and the weed flung against its side washes off again. But when he had no power to beat down their blind resolve, and the cruel will of Juno had its way, the old man called the gods and the empty air to witness again and again: "We are broken by fate," he cried, "swept off by the storm. You poor fools — you will pay for this with your own cursed blood. As for you, Turnus, a bitter punishment is coming, and you will pray to the gods too late. For me, my rest is won, my harbor in sight; I lose only the happiness of dying in peace." He said no more, but shut himself inside his walls and let the reins of state fall from his hands.

There was a custom in Latium of the West, which the Alban cities held sacred ever after, and which mighty Rome holds to this day, when men first rouse the war-god to battle — whether they make ready to carry grief and tears to the Getae, or the Arabs, or the Hyrcanians, or to march against the dawn and the Indians, and win back their lost standards from the Parthians. There are twin gates of War — that is their name — held in awe and dreaded for the savage god behind them; a hundred bars of bronze, the everlasting iron, lock them, and Janus never leaves the threshold, the watchman at the doors. When the elders have voted certainly for war, the consul himself, in the robe and the war-belt of Quirinus, swings the grinding hinges back and calls the men to battle, and all the army roars after him, and the brazen trumpets blow their rough agreement. By this rite Latinus too should have declared war on the men of Aeneas and unbarred the grim gates. But the old father would not lay his hand to them; he turned away from the hateful office and hid himself in the dark. Then the queen of the gods herself came gliding down from heaven, drove the lingering gates open with her own hand, and as she turned the hinge burst the iron bars of War. Italy, peaceful and still a moment before, took fire. Some made ready to march out on foot across the plains; some thundered up on their high horses in clouds of dust. Every man wanted his weapons. They rubbed the bright shields and the smooth spearheads slick with fat, ground the axes on the stone; they loved to lift the standards now and hear the trumpets call. Five great cities set up their anvils and forged new weapons — strong Atina, proud Tibur, Ardea, Crustumerium, and Antemnae crowned with towers. They hammered out helmets to guard the head, bent the willow into wicker shields; some beat out breastplates of bronze, or smooth greaves of soft silver. The honor of the plough-blade and the sickle, all the love of the field, gave way; they melted their fathers' swords down and forged them new. The trumpets sounded. The watchword went out to muster. One man snatched his helmet from the wall in a fury; another harnessed his stamping horses, pulled on his coat of gold-linked mail and his trusty sword, and buckled on his shield.

Now, Muses, open Helicon and start the song — tell which kings were stirred to war, what armies followed each one and filled the plains, what men even then flowered in Italy, that kind mother of harvests, what weapons burned in their hands. For you remember, goddesses, and you have the power to tell; to us only the faint breath of the story comes down. First into the war, fierce, came Mezentius from the Tuscan shore, a man who scorned the gods, and armed his men. Beside him his son Lausus, finest of them all but for the body of Turnus the Laurentine — Lausus, the breaker of horses and the master of game, who led a thousand men out of the city of Agylla, in vain; a son who deserved a happier father than Mezentius, and a father better than Mezentius to obey.

After them Aventinus, the beautiful son of beautiful Hercules, showed his palm-crowned chariot and his horses crowned for victory across the field, and wore his father's emblem on his shield — the hundred serpents and the snake-haired Hydra. The priestess Rhea bore him in secret, out in the woods on the Aventine hill, a woman lying with a god, after Hercules came triumphant from killing Geryon and touched the fields of Laurentum and bathed the Spanish cattle in the Tuscan river. His men carried javelins and cruel pikes into battle, and fought with the tapered sword and the Sabine spit. He himself went on foot, a great lion's skin swinging over his shoulders, its bristling pelt and its white teeth crowning his head — so he strode into the king's hall, savage, wrapped in the gear of Hercules.

Then two brothers left the walls of Tibur — the people take their name from their brother Tiburtus — Catillus and brave Coras, young men of Argos, and they rode into the thick of the spears in the front rank, like two cloud-born Centaurs coming down from a high mountain, leaving Homole and snowy Othrys behind them at a run; the great forest gives way as they go, and the thickets break apart with a crash before them.

Nor was the founder of Praeneste missing — Caeculus, the king whom every age has believed was born of Vulcan among the country herds and found beside the hearth. A long file of farmers follows him, gathered from high Praeneste and the fields of Juno of Gabii, from the cold river Anio and the dewy rocks of the Hernici, from rich Anagnia and from you, Father Amasenus. Not all of them have weapons or shields or rattling chariots; most of them sling bullets of dull lead, some carry a pair of darts apiece, and for caps they wear tawny wolfskin over their heads. The left foot goes bare as they march; the right is shod in raw oxhide. And Messapus, tamer of horses, son of Neptune, whom no man may bring down with fire or steel, called up suddenly to arms a people long unused to war, peoples that had forgotten the sword, and drew his blade again. He led the ranks of Fescennium and the just Faliscans, the men who hold Soracte's heights and the fields of Flavinium and Ciminus' lake and hill and the groves of Feronia. They marched in order, singing their king's praises as they went — the way the snow-white swans, among the streaming clouds, lift their song out of their soft throats coming home from feeding, and the Asian marsh far off rings with the answering cry. No one would have thought those columns an army of bronze; you would have called them a great cloud of harsh-voiced birds driving in off the deep sea toward the shore.

And look — Clausus, of the old Sabine blood, brought a great army with him, and was an army in himself; from him today the Claudian tribe and house is spread through Latium, since Rome was shared with the Sabines. With him came a vast cohort of Amiternum, the old men of Cures, all the men of Eretum and olive-bearing Mutusca; men who live in the town of Nomentum, in the Rosean country by Velinus, on the crags of rough Tetrica and Mount Severus, in Casperia and Foruli and along the river Himella; men who drink the Tiber and the Fabaris, men sent from cold Nursia, the squadrons of Horta and the Latin peoples, and the men the river Allia cut through with its unlucky name. As many as the waves that roll on the Libyan sea when fierce Orion sinks into the winter water, as thick as the ears of grain scorched ripe by the new sun on the Hermus plain or the yellow fields of Lycia — so many were they; their shields rang, and the ground shook, struck and trampled under their feet.

Next Halaesus, born of Agamemnon's line and an enemy to the very name of Troy, yoked his horses to the chariot and swept a thousand fierce peoples to Turnus' aid: the men who turn the Massic soil that is good for wine, and the men the Auruncan fathers sent down from the high hills, and their Sidicine neighbors from the plain, and the men of Cales, and the men who live by the shallow river Volturnus, and beside them the rough Saticulan and the Oscan ranks. Smooth round javelins are their weapons, but they fasten them with a strap to bring them back; their left arm carries a small shield, and they fight close in with the curved sword.

Nor will you go unsung in our verse, Oebalus — son, they say, of Telon and the nymph Sebethis, when Telon, old already, was king of Capreae; but his son, not content with his father's small kingdom, had spread his sway over the people of the Sarrastes and the plains the Sarnus waters, and over those who hold Rufrae and Batulum and the fields of Celemna, and the men under the apple-laden walls of high Abella. They throw the spear in the Teutonic way; for caps they strip the cork-tree's bark; their crescent shields flash bronze, and the sword flashes bronze.

And the mountains of Nursia sent you to the war, Ufens, famous and lucky in arms; your people the Aequi, hardest of all, hunting the woods always with their lances, scratching their stubborn ground in armor — it pleased them to live by plunder and on the spoils of the hunt. The priest Umbro came too, of the Marsi, sent by King Archippus, his helmet bound with sprigs of the blessed olive — a brave man, who with a charm and a touch of the hand could lay the snake-tribe and the foul-breathing water-serpents to sleep, soothe their fury and cure their bites with his art. But he found no charm against the wound of a Trojan spear-point; his sleep-songs and the herbs gathered on the Marsian hills were no use against it. For him the grove of Angitia wept, and the glass water of Fucinus, and the clear lakes.

Virbius went out too, the beautiful son of Hippolytus — sent to the war by Aricia his mother, raised in the wet groves of Egeria, where the rich altar of Diana stands kind to those who pray. The story goes that Hippolytus, when his stepmother's cunning destroyed him and he paid his father's anger with his blood, torn apart by his terrified horses, came back into the high air, under the stars, brought back to life by the herbs of the Healer and the love of Diana. Then the all-powerful Father, furious that any mortal should rise from the shadows of the dead into the light of life, struck the finder of that medicine, Apollo's son, down with his thunderbolt into the waters of the Styx. But kind Diana hid Hippolytus away in a secret place and gave him to the nymph Egeria and her grove, where he could live out his life alone and unknown in the Italian woods, and where, his name changed, they called him Virbius. That is why horned horses are kept far from the temple and the sacred grove of Diana, ever since they bolted in terror at the sea-monster and threw the young man and his chariot along the shore. His son drove fiery horses across the plain all the same, and rode his chariot to war.

And among them, in the front rank, Turnus himself moved, taller by a head than them all, gripping his weapons. His high helmet, with its triple plume, carried a Chimaera breathing Etna's fire from its mouth; the worse the battle raged and ran red, the more it roared with its savage flames. And on his polished shield was Io, lifting her gilded horns, already turned to a heifer, already covered in bristling hide — a great theme — and Argus her guard, and her father Inachus pouring his river from a carved urn. A cloud of foot soldiers came behind him, and shield-bearing columns filled the whole plain: the young men of Argos, the Auruncan bands, the Rutulians, the old Sicanians, the Sacranian ranks, the Labici with their painted shields; men who plough your woods, Tiber, and the holy bank of Numicus; men whose ploughshare works the Rutulian hills and Circe's headland, the fields where Jupiter of Anxur watches over them and Feronia rejoices in her green grove; men from the black marsh of Satura and the cold valley where the Ufens looks for his way to the sea and sinks at last under it.

And last of all came Camilla, of the Volscian people, leading her column of cavalry, her squadrons bright with bronze — a warrior. She had never trained her woman's hands to the distaff or the wool-baskets of Minerva; she was a girl made to bear the hard work of battle and to outrun the wind. She could have flown over the standing grain at the top of the field and never bruised the tender ears as she ran; she could have skimmed the swell of the open sea and held her course, and never wet her flying feet in the water. The whole countryside poured out of the houses and the fields to watch her pass, the young men and the crowd of mothers, and stared in wonder, struck dumb, as she went by — the royal purple draped over her smooth shoulders, a brooch of gold catching up her hair, and on her back the Lycian quiver and the shepherd's myrtle staff tipped with a spear.

sections.label: Book VIII
sections.title: Evander, and the Shield of Aeneas

segments.text: When Turnus ran up the war-flag on the towers of Laurentum, and the harsh trumpets blared, and he lashed his eager horses and clashed his weapons, every heart was stirred at once. All Latium rose in a panic and swore itself to the cause; the young men raged for the fight. Their chief captains — Messapus, Ufens, and Mezentius, who scorned the gods — drew their forces from every side and stripped the wide fields of their farmhands for soldiers. And they sent Venulus to the city of Diomedes to beg for help, to tell him the Trojans had landed in Latium, that Aeneas had come with his beaten fleet and his exiled gods and now claimed Italy as his own, saying fate had given it to him; that many peoples were rallying to the man, and his name was spreading through the land. What he was building toward, what disaster might follow if luck went his way — Diomedes could weigh that better than Turnus or King Latinus could.

So it stood with the Latins. And the Trojan hero saw the whole storm coming and was tossed on a great tide of worry. His mind darted one way, then another, snatched at this plan and that, turned the trouble over and over and could find no rest — the way light off water in a bronze basin, thrown back by the sun or the bright face of the moon, flickers and skips across a whole room, leaps up of a sudden and trembles on the high paneled ceiling. It was night, and across the wide world a tired sleep held the birds of the air and the beasts; and Aeneas, his heart heavy with the thought of war, lay down on the bank of the Tiber under the cold sky and gave his body, late, to rest.

Then the god of the place himself, old Tiberinus of the lovely river, seemed to rise up among the poplar leaves; fine linen, sea-green, draped him, and a crown of shadowy reeds covered his hair. And he spoke, and his words took the grief away: "Seed of the line of gods, you who carry Troy back to us out of the hands of her enemies, who keep her citadel alive forever — this is the soil you were promised, this the home that has waited for you; do not turn back. The anger of the gods has settled; the swelling rage is spent. And so you will not think a dream has made all this up out of nothing: under the oaks along the shore you will find a great white sow lying with her thirty young, white like her, gathered at her teats. This is the place your city will stand. This is the sure end of your labors. From this sign, when thirty years have rolled around, your son Ascanius will found a city of shining name — Alba.

"What I tell you is true. Now hear how to come through what is coming. An Arcadian people, the sons of Pallas, who followed King Evander here when he was driven from his own land, have chosen a spot in these hills and built a town and called it Pallanteum, after their forefather Pallas. They are forever at war with the Latins. Take these men into your camp as allies; bind a treaty with them. I myself will lead you up my banks and straight along my stream, so your oars can drive against the current. Rise up, son of Venus, and as the first stars are setting, make your prayers to Juno, as the rite demands, and beat down her anger and her threats with vows of submission. When you have won your war, pay me what is owed. I am the one you see brushing these banks with my full flood, cutting through the rich farmland — the dark Tiber, the river heaven loves best. Here is my great house. From here my waters will one day wash the walls of mighty Rome." So the river-god spoke, and sank down into the deep pool, and the night and the dream both let Aeneas go.

He rose, and looked up, and saw the dawn flushing the sky. He cupped water from the Tiber in his hands, the rite's own way, and poured out his prayers to heaven: "You nymphs of Laurentum, you who feed the rivers, and you, father Tiber, with your sacred stream — take Aeneas in at last, and keep him from harm. Wherever your waters rise, whatever spring or pool holds them hidden, you who pity our long suffering, you king of the horned floods — I will honor you, I will keep your name with offerings forever. Only be with my people; make good the promise you made." So he prayed; then he picked two galleys from his fleet, fitted them with oars, and armed his men. And then — a thing to marvel at — there on the green bank lay the sow, white, with her white young around her teats, just as the god had said. Dutiful Aeneas took her and her whole brood and laid them on Juno's altar; to you, great Juno, to you he made the sacrifice.

All that long night the Tiber smoothed his swelling stream; he flowed back on himself and held still, hushing his water to the calm of a standing pool, a quiet marsh, so that there was no fight against the oar. The Trojans pushed off and made their way, and the ship slid over the shallows almost without effort; the woods and the waters marveled at the strange sight — the shields flashing, the painted hulls afloat on a river. One whole night and a day they rowed on, up through the green shade, and cut the still water. The sun had climbed to the height of noon when they saw, far off, walls and a fort and a scatter of rooftops — what Roman power has since raised level with the sky, but which then was only Evander's small holding, a poor man's estate. They turned their prows for the shore. It happened that the Arcadian king, that very day, was paying the rite he owed to great Hercules, the son of Amphitryon, and to all the gods, in a grove outside the town. His son Pallas was with him, and the chief young men, and his poor senate; they were burning incense, and the warm blood still smoked on the altars.

But when they saw the tall ships gliding up through the shadowed trees, the Arcadians sprang to their feet, alarmed, and broke off the feast. Bold Pallas would not have the rites abandoned; he snatched up a spear and ran alone to meet the strangers, and called from a rise of ground: "Men — what brings you down these unknown waters? Where are you bound? What is your race, what is your home? Do you come in peace, or with war?" High on the stern, father Aeneas stood and held out a branch of peace-bearing olive in his hand: "You see men born of Troy, and weapons that are no friend to the Latins, who drove us to war though we came in peace. We are looking for Evander. Tell him this: the leaders of Troy have come asking for an alliance." Pallas was struck dumb at so great a name. "Whoever you are, come ashore," he said. "Come, speak to my father face to face, and be our guest." He gave the prince his hand and led him up from the water into the grove.

There Aeneas spoke first to the king: "Best of the Greeks, to you fate has sent me holding these branches of peace. I came without fear, though I know your blood is Greek, and your line runs back to Atreus and the two kings of his house. My own worth, your great name, the old kinship of our fathers, and the word of Apollo brought me here — by choice, not only by need. Our founder Dardanus, born of Electra, came from the loins of Atlas, the same Atlas who holds the sky on his shoulder; and your father is Mercury, whom Maia bore on the cold height of Cyllene — Maia, Atlas's daughter. So our two houses spring from one source. Trusting that, I sent no envoy ahead, I asked no leave; I came myself, my own messenger, with my life in my hands. The same Rutulians who hunt us hunt you too. If they drive us out, nothing will stop them from holding all Italy from sea to sea. Take our hand, and give us yours. We have stout hearts and strong arms for the war; we have been tried, and we have held."

Aeneas had been watching the man's face and his eyes all the while he spoke, the whole of him. When he finished Evander answered, short and warm: "How gladly I take you in, bravest of the Trojans! How your face brings back your father's — I can still see Anchises in your every look and gesture. I remember it well: Priam came once through this country, going to visit his sister's court, and Anchises came with him. I was only a boy, with the first down on my cheeks, and I marveled at all those great men; but Anchises towered over the rest, and my young heart burned to take his hand. I did, in the end; I brought him home with me, and when he had to go he gave me a fine Lycian quiver, a Cretan bow, an embroidered cloak, and two golden bridles my son's horses still wear. So the alliance you ask, I give. Tomorrow, when the sun is up, I will send you off with men. For now, honor our yearly feast with us — these are rites no delay should keep us from — and take your place at a humble table among friends." He had the cups and the food brought back, and seated the Trojans himself on the grass; for Aeneas alone he spread a lion's shaggy hide over a maple chair. They ate roasted meat and bread, and the priest poured the wine.

When the worst of the hunger was eased, Evander said: "These rites of ours, this altar, this feast — they are not some empty superstition, nor blind habit. We keep them because we were saved, and we are grateful, and we pay back what a god did for us. Look at that crag over there, hung against the sky, with the heaps of rubble at its foot and the cave standing bare and ruined. That was once the den of Cacus, a half-man, half-beast, a thing the sun never reached. The ground at his door was always wet with fresh slaughter, and men's faces hung nailed to the posts, pale with rotting gore. His father was Vulcan, and like his father he breathed black smoke and gouts of fire as he dragged his huge bulk around. But the time came at last that brought us a god. Hercules came through, in triumph, having killed the three-bodied giant Geryon in Spain and driven off his great herd of cattle; and he turned them loose to graze here by the Tiber.

"But Cacus, mad for plunder and ready for any crime, made off with four prize bulls and as many heifers — and so there would be no tracks pointing the right way, he dragged them backward by the tail into his cave, the hoofprints all turned around, and shut them in the dark rock. Whoever came searching, the signs led him nowhere. By and by Hercules was moving his well-fed herd on to fresh pasture, and as the cattle bellowed at leaving, one heifer answered from deep in the cave and lowed, and that single penned-up call gave Cacus away. Hercules blazed with a black, savage rage. He caught up his knotted club and ran for the high mountain — and then, for the first time, we saw the monster afraid, fear in his eyes, his face gone white, faster on his feet than the wind. He threw himself down into his hole and slammed the great rock door his father had hung on iron chains, snapped the chains, and dropped it home.

"But there came the Avenger, raging round the cave, turning his eyes this way and that, gnashing his teeth. Three times, hot with anger, he circled the whole of the Aventine; three times he heaved at the cave-mouth and failed and fell back, panting. There was a spike of black flint at the back of the mountain, sheer, a roost for birds of ill omen, leaning out over the river. Hercules braced his feet on the right, took hold of it, and wrenched — and the rock tore loose from its roots, and the sky thundered at the shock, and the banks leapt apart, and the terrified river ran backward. The whole court of Cacus stood open to the day; the dark den glared in the new light, the way the earth might crack and lay hell bare to heaven, and the ghosts shrink back, hating the sun that has broken in on their night. Caught in the open, with no way out, the monster howled an unmanly howl, and Hercules rained stones and spears down on him. Cacus, with nowhere left, belched a vast cloud of smoke from his throat — a thing to wonder at — and wrapped the cave in a blind black murk, so no eye could find him. But the god leapt down through it, through the fume, where the smoke rolled thickest, half-blind, half-choked, and groped his way, and got his hands on the beast. He twisted him into a knot and clung and choked him till the eyes burst from his head and the throat ran dry of blood. Then he tore the doors open and let in the day, and dragged out the stolen cattle and the foul carcass by the feet, and the whole countryside came to gape at the giant's shaggy chest and his dead-out eyes and the mouth that breathed fire no more. From that day we have kept the rite, and Potitius first set up these yearly vows, with the house of the Pinarii to keep them. So crown your heads, young men, fill the cups, and call together on the god who keeps us safe."

When he had said this, the evening star was already climbing the sky. The priests went in procession, Potitius at their head, wrapped in the skins of beasts and carrying torches; they laid the second course on the tables and heaped the platters at the altar. The leaping Salii came to sing around the kindled fires, their temples bound with poplar — one choir of old men, one of the young — and they sang the deeds of Hercules: how as a baby in his cradle he strangled the two serpents Juno sent; how he broke Troy and Oechalia; the thousand trials Eurystheus and Juno's hate piled on him; how his unbeaten hands brought down the cloud-born Centaurs, the Cretan bull, the great lion, the Hydra of Lerna with its hissing heads; how the three-throated hound of hell lay fawning at his feet, and the rivers of the dead shook at the sight of him. "Hail, true son of Jupiter, glory added to the gods! Come to us and to your rites with a kind step, an answering grace." So they sang, and over all the rest they crowned the feast with the den and the death of Cacus, and the hollow valleys carried the sound, and the hills threw it back.

Then, the rites done, they all walked back toward the town, and Evander between young Pallas and the old king led the way, easing the road with talk. Aeneas turned his eyes everywhere, taken with each new thing, and asked, glad and curious, about all of it — the relics, the works of the men of old. And Evander, founder of what would be the towers of Rome, said: "These woods were the home of native Fauns and Nymphs, and of a race of men sprung from tree-trunks and hard oak, who had no law, no settled ways, who could not yoke an ox or store what they had; the wild hunt fed them, and the running streams. Then Saturn came, fleeing the weapons of Jupiter, an exile from his stolen kingdom. He gathered that scattered, hill-bred people, gave them laws, and chose the name Latium for the land — the land where he had lain hidden, safe. Under his reign were the ages men call golden, and he ruled the peoples in deep peace, until little by little a baser, tarnished age came on, with the madness of war and the hunger to have. Then the Ausonians came, and the Sicanians, and the land changed its name many times over, and harsh kings ruled it, the giant Thybris among them, who gave his name to our river, the Tiber, that men once called Albula. And I came last of all, driven from my own country across the seas, sent here by all-powerful Fortune and the word of heaven, on my mother the nymph's warning."

So talking he went on, and showed him the gate the Romans would one day call Carmental, after old Carmentis the prophetess, who first sang of the great sons of Aeneas to come and of noble Pallanteum. He showed him the wide grove Romulus would make his sanctuary, and the Lupercal under the cold rock, named in the old Arcadian way for Lycaean Pan; he showed him the wood of the Argiletum, and told the tale of his murdered guest Argus. From there he led him up to the Tarpeian height and the Capitol — golden now, but in those days rough and bristling with woodland thickets. Even then a dread holiness about the place frightened the country folk; even then they trembled at the wood and the rock. "Some god lives in this grove, on this leafy hill," Evander said, "though no one knows which. The Arcadians believe they have seen Jupiter himself, shaking the dark storm-cloud of his shield in his right hand and calling up the rain." Then he showed him two towns with their walls thrown down, the wreckage and memorials of the men of old: Janus had founded the one, Saturn the other, and they were called Janiculum and Saturnia. Talking so between them, they came up to the house of poor Evander, and everywhere they went they saw cattle lowing — in the Roman Forum, and in the fine quarter of the Carinae. At the door he said: "Hercules himself, in his triumph, stooped under this lintel; this little house took him in. Dare, my guest, to think nothing of wealth; shape yourself, as he did, into a man worthy of a god, and do not come to our poor table looking down on it." And he led great Aeneas in under the low roof and laid him on a bed of strewn leaves and a Libyan bear's hide.

Night came down and folded the earth in her dark wings. But Venus, frightened for her son — for the new war, and the rising threats, were no idle fear — lay close beside Vulcan in their golden bed, and breathed the charm of love into every word: "While the Greeks and cruel fate were leveling the towers of Troy, I asked you for nothing, no help to save the doomed, no work of your skill — though I owed much to Priam's house, and grieved hard for all Aeneas suffered. But now, by Jupiter's command and the will of fate, his line is set to reign in Italy; and so I come to you, a mother kneeling for her son, to beg the art that is yours. Thetis once moved you to forge arms, and the Dawn for her son; now look how many fierce nations are bound together against what is left of Troy, sword and fire ready to destroy my people — to conquer Venus a second time, in conquering them again." So she spoke, and folded her snow-white arms around him as he held back, and warmed him into yielding. He took the old flame at once; the familiar heat went into his marrow and ran through his loosened bones, the way a thread of fire darts through the storm-clouds in a flash of thunder. The goddess felt it, and knew her beauty had won, and smiled.

Then Vulcan, helpless under her charm, said: "Why look so far for reasons? Where has your faith in me gone, your faith in your own beauty? Long ago, if you had asked, I could have armed your Trojans — neither Jupiter nor fate forbade Troy ten more years. And now, if you mean to make war, whatever care my craft can promise, whatever can be made of iron or of molten gold, all that fire and the breath of the bellows can do — it is yours. Stop pleading as if you doubted your own power." And with that he took the willing goddess in his arms and gave himself to a deep and easy sleep. Then, when the first rest had passed and the night had run half its course — the hour when a poor housewife wakes to wake the embers and rouse her maids to the wool and the loom, working by lamplight to keep her household fed and her marriage-bed honest — at that same hour the Lord of the Fire rose from his soft couch to his work.

There is an island that rises sheer with smoking rocks between Sicily and Aeolian Lipari, and beneath it the caves of Aetna, hollowed out for the Cyclopes' forges, thunder. This is Vulcan's house, and the land bears his name. Here he came down through the dark air. The Cyclopes were working the iron in the vast cave — Brontes and Steropes and Pyracmon with his bare arms. They had a thunderbolt half-shaped in their hands, polished in part — one of the many Jupiter hurls down on the world from every quarter of the sky. Three spokes of twisted hail they had put into it, three of rain-cloud, three of red fire, three of the winged South Wind; and now they were working in the terrible flashes, and the noise, and the dread, and the anger with its hounding flames. Elsewhere others were mending the war-chariot of Mars, the wheels he drives to rouse men and cities; and others burnished the dreadful shield of Minerva, the scaly snakes of gold, the writhing serpents, and the Gorgon's severed head with its rolling, dying eyes.

"Clear it all away," Vulcan called. "Set your tasks aside, Cyclopes of Aetna, and turn your minds to this: arms for a brave man. Now you need all your strength, all your speed, all the skill of your hands. Lose no time." That was all; and they bent at once to the work, sharing it out evenly. The bronze ran in streams, and gold, and the deadly steel melted in the great furnace. They shaped a vast shield, a single shield to stand against all the weapons of the Latins, and welded its seven rounds together. Some pumped the air in the wheezing bellows; some dipped the hissing bronze in the trough; the cave groaned under the anvils. They lifted their arms in turn, in time, and turned the glowing mass with the gripping tongs.

While the Lord of Lemnos drove the work on, the kindly morning and the song of the small birds woke Evander in his low house. The old man got up, drew on his tunic and tied his sandals, slung his good sword at his side, threw a panther's hide over his shoulder, and went out, two dogs going before him at the door, to find his royal guest. He had not forgotten the help he had promised, and he met Aeneas already coming to meet him, with young Pallas at his side and faithful Achates at the Trojan's. They clasped hands and sat down apart, and Evander spoke first: "Greatest of the Trojans — while you live I will never believe the cause of Troy is lost. But the help I can give from my own hand is small. On this side the Tiber pens us in; on that, the Latins press our walls and waste our fields. But I mean to join you with mighty nations, a camp rich with kingdoms — a chance fortune has dropped in your way. Not far from here stands an old and famous town, Agylla, that the Lydian people built long ago among the hills; the Greeks called it Caere. It flourished a long time, until the cruel Mezentius seized the crown and ruled it with a heavy, brutal hand.

"How can I tell you the unspeakable murders, the savage deeds of that tyrant? May the gods turn them back on his own head and his children's! He bound dead men to the living — fastened them hand to hand and face to face, a new kind of torture — and so, in that foul embrace, dripping with rot and gore, he killed his victims by a long, slow dying. At last the people had enough; they took up arms and surrounded his palace, cut down his men, and fired the house, and he broke through the crowd and fled in the dark to Turnus, who took him in. So all Etruria has risen in a just rage and demands her king back for punishment, and stands ready to sail; and over these thousands I will set you in command. Their ships crowd the shore, the men cry to weigh anchor — but an old soothsayer holds them back, chanting the fates: 'Lydian chiefs, flower of the old Etruscan stock, whom a just anger arms against Mezentius — no man of Italy may lead so great a people. Look for a foreign captain.' So they wait, awed by the word, on the beach, longing for their promised leader. Tarchon, the Etruscan chief, has sent me their crown and their royal robes, asking me to take the throne and lead them. But the cold blood of age, and my tired limbs, and a heart that knows its own decline, forbid me a crown now. I would put my son forward — but his mother is a Sabine, and half his blood is of this land. You are the man: a foreign line and a man's full strength, called by fate and by fortune both. Take him with you, my Pallas, the staff and hope of my last years; let him learn war at your side, his eyes on your courage. I give him two hundred horse, my own, the best I have, and Pallas adds two hundred more in his own name."

He had hardly finished when Aeneas and faithful Achates dropped their eyes, and a heavy grief came over them — short of help, and braced for so hard a war — until Venus sent a sign from a clear sky: a thunderclap rolled three times overhead, and the lightning flashed three times, and the blast of a war-trumpet rang from the air. They looked up; and again and again the peals came; and there, in the still bright heaven, arms began to shine through a cloud and to clash, a metal music. The rest stood trembling, struck with awe; but Aeneas knew the sign for his own. "Do not be afraid," he said to Evander. "This is for me. Heaven is calling me to the war. My goddess mother foretold she would send this sign if war came on, and bring me arms forged by Vulcan through the air to help me. What slaughter waits, now, for the wretched Latins! What a price Turnus will pay! How many bodies and shields and helmets you will roll down to the sea, father Tiber! Let them break the treaty. Let them call for war."

When he had said this he rose, and first he woke the dying fire on Hercules's altar and gladly sought again the household gods he had honored the day before; and Evander and the Trojans together offered their chosen sheep. Then Aeneas went down to his ships and his men, and picked out the best of them to go with him to war, while the rest drifted down the easy current to carry the news to Ascanius and his father's plans. The Trojans who would ride to the Etruscan land were given horses; for Aeneas they brought the finest of them, draped in a lion's skin that flashed with gilded claws. The word ran through the little town that horsemen were riding fast to the king of the Etruscans, and the mothers, in their fear, doubled their prayers, and the danger loomed larger, and the face of war came nearer.

Then old Evander caught his son in a long embrace, and would not let go, and the tears ran down. "If only Jupiter would give me back the years I have lost — the man I was under the walls of Praeneste, when I burned whole heaps of captured shields and sent King Erulus down to the dead with my own hand, the man his mother Feronia had given three lives and three sets of arms, so I had to kill him three times over — if I were that man again, no danger, no death, would tear me from your arms, my Pallas, and Mezentius would not have boasted so long unpunished, would not have piled the dead so high. You gods, and you, great Jupiter, pity an old man and a king. If fate means to bring my boy home safe, if I am to see him again — then keep me alive, let me bear any pain, in the hope of holding him once more. But if some unspeakable blow is coming, then let me break off this cruel life now, now, while my fears are still in doubt, while the future is uncertain, while I hold you, dear boy, my one late joy, here in my arms — before any word of grief can reach me." So the father poured out his heart at the last parting; then he fainted, and his servants carried him into the house.

Now the horsemen rode out through the open gates, Aeneas at their head with Achates beside him, the other Trojan captains next, and Pallas in the middle of the column, bright in his armor and his embroidered cloak, like the morning star fresh from the sea — the star Venus loves above the rest — lifting his holy face in the sky and melting the dark. On the walls the trembling mothers followed the dust-cloud with their eyes, watching the bronze flash through it. The troop took the shortest road over the brush and the open country; the shouting rose, the column formed, and the hooves of the horses shook the dry ground. There is a cool dark grove by the river near the Etruscan town, hallowed long ago, ringed with gloomy hills — the first Greek settlers gave it to Silvanus, god of the fields and the flocks. Near it, in a safe camp, Tarchon and his Etruscans lay; and from a rise Aeneas saw the whole army spread across the plain. There he led his weary men and rested them, and fed the tired horses.

Meanwhile Venus, bright through the clouds, came bearing the gifts, and found her son alone in a quiet fold of the valley by the cold river. She showed herself plain before him, no disguise, and said: "Here is what I promised, finished by Vulcan's hand. Now go, and do not be slow to challenge the proud Latins, or Turnus himself, to the field." She embraced him, and set the shining arms under an oak before him. He could not have enough of looking at the goddess's gift; he turned it over, lifted it, weighed it in his hands, marveling — the crested helmet that spat fire, the deadly sword, the stiff bronze of the breastplate, blood-red and huge, like a dark cloud lit from within by the sun; the smooth greaves of gold and electrum, the spear, and last of all the shield, beyond any telling.

There the Lord of the Fire had wrought the story of Italy and the triumphs of Rome — for he knew the prophets, and he was not ignorant of the age to come. There were all the sons of Ascanius's line, the generations down the years, and the wars they would fight, each one in order. He had made the she-wolf, just delivered, lying in the green cave of Mars; the twin boys hung playing at her teats and mouthed her without fear, and she, her sleek neck bent back, licked them by turns and shaped their small bodies with her tongue. Near that he set Rome, and the Sabine women carried off against all custom from the crowded seats at the games; and then the war that flared up between Romulus and old Tatius; and then the two kings, the fighting done, standing armed at the altar of Jupiter, cups in their hands, sealing a treaty over a slain sow. Close by, two teams of four horses had torn Mettus apart, dragged opposite ways — but you should have kept your word, man of Alba — and Tullus hauled the liar's flesh through a wood, and the briars dripped with his blood.

And there was Porsenna, ordering Rome to take the banished Tarquin back, hemming the city with a great siege, while the sons of Aeneas threw themselves on the sword for liberty; you could see him drawn to the life, swollen with anger and threats, because Cocles dared to break the bridge, and Cloelia broke her chains and swam the river. At the top of the shield, Manlius, the watchman of the Tarpeian fort, stood before the temple and held the high Capitol; and there, fluttering through the gilded porticoes, the silver goose cried out that the Gauls were at the gate. The Gauls were in the thickets, close, taking the citadel under cover of the dark and the gift of the murky night — gold their hair, gold their dress, their striped cloaks shining, their milk-white necks ringed with gold, two Alpine pikes flashing in each man's hand, the long shields slung at their arms. There too he had hammered out the leaping Salii and the naked Luperci, the wool-tufted caps, and the sacred shields fallen from heaven; and the chaste matrons leading the holy rites through the city in their soft litters. Far off he set the halls of Tartarus too, the high gates of hell, and the punishments of crime — and you, Catiline, hanging on a beetling crag and shuddering at the faces of the Furies — and, set apart, the righteous, with Cato giving them their laws.

And between these scenes ran a sea of swelling gold, the blue waves whitening with foam, and bright dolphins, wrought in silver, sweeping their tails through the water in a ring. In the center were the bronze-clad fleets, the battle of Actium: you could see all Leucate boiling with the war and the waves ablaze with gold. On this side Augustus Caesar, leading the men of Italy into battle with the Senate and the People, the household gods and the great gods beside him, stood high on the stern; twin flames of joy streamed from his temples, and his father's star rose over his head. Near him Agrippa, towering, with the wind and the gods behind him, drove his line on, the beaked naval crown — proud emblem of war — shining at his brow. On the other side, with all his barbarian wealth and his motley arms, came Antony, victor over the peoples of the East and the Red Sea shore, bringing Egypt with him, and the powers of the Orient, and farthest Bactria — and following him, the horror of it, his Egyptian wife.

They came on, all at once; the whole sea churned to foam under the dragging oars and the three-pronged prows. They made for the deep — you would think the Cyclades had been torn loose and were floating on the water, or that mountain crashed against mountain, so huge were the towering ships the men drove at one another. Burning tow and flying iron showered down, and the fields of Neptune ran red with fresh slaughter. In the midst the queen called her squadrons on with the rattle of her country's sistrum — and did not yet look back at the two snakes behind her. Monstrous gods of every shape, and barking Anubis, leveled their weapons against Neptune and Venus and Minerva. Mars raged in the thick of the fight, graven in iron, and the grim Furies swept down from the sky, and Discord strode by in a torn robe, glad of the ruin, with Bellona at her heels swinging a bloody whip. And Apollo of Actium, watching from above, bent his bow over it all; and at that terror every Egyptian and Indian, every Arab and Sabaean, turned to flee. The queen herself seemed to call up the winds and spread her sails and let the sheets run slack; the Lord of the Fire had shown her amid the slaughter, pale with the death that was coming, carried out to sea on the wind and the wave; and across from her, the Nile, mourning, his great body stretched wide, opening the folds of his robe and calling the beaten home with all his garment into his blue lap and his sheltering streams.

But Caesar, riding into the walls of Rome in a triple triumph, was paying his deathless vow to the gods of Italy — three hundred great shrines through the whole city. The streets roared with joy and games and applause; in every temple a choir of matrons, an altar at every door, slain bullocks strewing the ground. Caesar himself, seated at the snow-white threshold of shining Apollo, looked over the gifts of the nations and hung them on the proud doorposts, while the conquered peoples filed past in a long line, as different in dress and arms as in tongue — the loose-robed Africans and the Nomads, the Leleges and the Carians, the arrow-bearing Geloni; the Euphrates flowing humbler now, and the two-horned Rhine, the far Dahae, and the Araxes chafing under its new bridge.

Such were the scenes across the shield of Vulcan, his mother's gift. Aeneas marveled at them, glad in the pictures though he could not read what they meant — and he lifted onto his shoulder the fame and the fate of his descendants.

sections.label: Book IX
sections.title: Turnus at the Walls, and the Night of Nisus and Euryalus

segments.text: While all this was happening far away, Juno sent Iris down out of heaven to bold Turnus. He was sitting apart, alone, in a sacred grove that had belonged to his ancestor Pilumnus, deep in his own thoughts. And Iris, daughter of Thaumas, spoke to him with her rose-colored lips: "Turnus — what no god would have dared to promise you if you'd prayed for it, the turning day has handed you for free. Aeneas has left his city, his men, his fleet, and gone off to the court of King Evander, far up the Tiber, to the Arcadian settlements. And not content with that, he's pushed on into the farthest Etruscan towns, raising an army out of their farmers. So why wait? This is the hour. Call for the horses and the chariots. Break off your delay, and take their camp while it's caught off guard." She finished, and rose into the sky on level wings, cutting the great arc of her rainbow through the clouds as she climbed. Turnus knew her, and lifted both hands to the light, and called after her as she fled: "Iris, glory of the sky — who sent you down to me through the clouds, down to the earth? Why has the weather broken open so suddenly? I can see the heart of the sky tearing apart, and the stars wandering loose at the pole. I'll follow the sign, whoever you are who calls me to arms." And with that he went to the river, scooped up water in his hands, and prayed long to the gods above, loading the air with his vows.

Then the whole army was on the move across the open plain, rich in horses, rich in embroidered cloaks and gold. Messapus led the front; the sons of Tyrrhus brought up the rear; and in the center came Turnus himself, the commander, a head taller than the rest, weapon in hand. So the deep Ganges rises in silence, fed by seven quiet streams, or the Nile, when its rich flood ebbs back from the fields and sinks again into its channel. The Trojans saw it from the walls — a sudden black cloud of dust gathering, a darkness rolling up over the plain. Caicus was the first to shout it from the rampart facing the enemy: "Men — what's that mass of dark coming on toward us? Quick, your swords, your spears, up onto the walls! The enemy's here, the enemy's here!" And with a great roar the Trojans poured in through all the gates and filled the walls. For Aeneas, their wise commander, had given the order before he left: if anything happened while he was away, they were not to draw up a line and risk open battle in the field; they were only to hold the camp, safe behind their walls and their banked-up works. So now, though shame and anger urged them to fight, they did as they were told. They shut the gates, and waited in their towers, under arms, for the enemy to come to them.

Turnus had flown ahead of the slow column, and now he came galloping up to the camp with twenty picked horsemen — sudden, unlooked for, on a dappled Thracian stallion, his helmet gold, its crest blood-red. "Who's with me?" he shouted. "Who'll be first against the enemy?" And he flung a javelin spinning into the sky, the opening shot of the war, and rode forward across the field while his men roared behind him. He was amazed to find the Trojans had no fight in them — that they wouldn't come out and meet him man to man on the level ground, but huddled inside their fort. So he rode up and down, raging, hunting for a way in where there was none. He was like a wolf prowling a full sheepfold in the dead of night, howling at the gaps, soaked by the wind and the rain, while the lambs bleat safe under their mothers; and he grinds his teeth, savage with a hunger he can't reach, his throat dry with the old craving and no blood in it. That was Turnus, burning as he stared at the walls, the fury rising in his hard bones — how to get at them, how to shake the cooped-up Trojans out into the open. Then he saw the fleet, drawn up close against the camp, hemmed in by the earthworks and the river that washed its flank, and he went for it. He called to his cheering men for fire, and his own fist closed hot around a blazing pine-brand. They threw themselves into it — his presence drove them — and every man armed himself with a torch snatched from the fires. The smoking pitch-pine threw up a black, greasy smoke shot through with sparks, and the cloud of it rolled up toward the stars.

What god, Muses, turned that fire away from the Trojan ships? Who saved the fleet from burning? The story is old, but its fame will never die. Back when Aeneas was first building this fleet on the slopes of Mount Ida, getting ready to put out to sea, they say the great Mother of the Gods herself, Cybele, came to her son Jupiter and said: "Grant your dear mother this one thing, now that you rule Olympus. There was a stand of pine I loved, a grove on the top of Ida — they brought me offerings there for years, dark with firs and maple, shadowed and holy. I gave that wood gladly to the young Trojan when he needed ships. But now I'm sick with fear for it. Take the fear from me. Let no storm wreck those ships, no gale drive them under. It should count for something that they grew on a mountain of mine." And her son, who turns the wheeling stars, answered her: "Mother, what are you asking the fates to do? You want ships built by human hands to last forever? You want Aeneas to cross uncertain seas with a certainty no mortal gets? What god has that kind of power? No. But this much I can grant: when they've done their work and reached their harbor in Italy, every ship that comes through the storms and carries Aeneas safe to the Laurentine fields — I'll strip its mortal shape away and turn it into a goddess of the deep sea, to swim the water like the Nereids do." And to seal it he swore by the river of his brother's kingdom, by the banks of pitch and the black flood of Styx, and bent his head, and all of heaven shook.

Now the appointed day had come. The fates had wound their thread out to the mark, and Cybele's hour was here — the moment to drive Turnus's torches off her holy ships. First a strange light flashed across the sky from the east and ran down it; then out of the clouds came a great noise, drums and the wild music of the Mother's worship rolling from Mount Ida; and a voice fell through the air on both armies at once, terrible to Trojan and Rutulian alike: "Trojans, don't rush to defend my ships. Don't take up arms for them. Turnus will set the sea itself on fire before he burns my sacred pines. And you — go free. Go, goddesses of the sea. The Mother commands it." And on the instant every ship snapped the cable that held it, dipped its prow like a dolphin, and dove under — and rose again, transformed: where the tall hulls had ridden at anchor, now that many maiden faces broke the water and swam out to sea. The Rutulians stood frozen in horror. Even Messapus was shaken, his horses balking under him; and the river itself, old Tiber, checked his current with a hoarse roar and drew his waters back from the sea.

But Turnus's nerve held. He rallied them, even rebuked them: "It's the Trojans those omens threaten, not us. Jupiter himself has taken away the one thing they could have run to. They didn't even wait for our swords and our fire — their own ships have abandoned them. The sea's no road for them now; there's no escape that way. Half the world is closed to them, and the land is ours — thousands of us in arms all around them. Their famous fate, their oracles, mean nothing to me. They got what fate gave them: they reached Italy, they touched the soil. Well, I have a fate of my own — to wipe out this criminal race that stole my bride. And it isn't only the sons of Atreus who feel that wrong; it isn't only Greeks who have the right to take up arms over it. 'Once destroyed is enough,' you'll say. They should have learned, then, the first time, to loathe every woman alive. These are men who put their trust in a wall between them and us — one thin ditch — as if that were any distance at all from death. Didn't they watch Troy go down in flames, and Troy was built by the hands of gods? So which of you, my brave men, will help me tear that rampart down and storm the camp while their courage shakes? I don't need a thousand ships, or the armor Vulcan forged. Let every Etruscan in Italy join them, for all I care. And let them not be afraid of the dark — no one's going to creep in and steal their luck the way they stole the Palladium, or murder their watchmen on the citadel. We won't hide inside a wooden horse. We'll do it in broad daylight, in the open, and we'll ring their walls with fire. I'll make them see they're not facing some pack of Greeks, the boys Hector held off for ten long years. Now — the better part of the day is gone. What's left of it, men, rest. You've done well. Look to your bodies, and be ready: the fight is coming."

Meanwhile the job of setting the watch and ringing the camp with sentries went to Messapus, and of feeding the night-fires. Fourteen Rutulian captains were chosen to keep guard at the walls, each with a hundred men behind him, every one of them helmeted, crested, flashing with gold. They spread out, took their stations, stretched on the grass; they drank, they tipped the wine-bowls, they kept the fires up. And the Trojans watched from above — they manned the walls in arms, and they checked the gates, anxious and awake, throwing up bridges from tower to tower and stockpiling weapons. Mnestheus drove them, and fierce Serestus, the two men Aeneas had left in charge of the camp and its young soldiers if anything went wrong. Up and down the walls the whole company drew lots for the watches and took their turns, each man covering his share of the danger.

Nisus was on guard at one of the gates — the keenest fighter of them all, son of Hyrtacus, sent to join Aeneas by Ida the huntress, quick with the javelin and the light arrow. Beside him was his friend Euryalus, the most beautiful of all who wore Trojan arms, a boy whose cheeks had only just begun to darken with the first beard. The two of them shared one love and went into every fight together, and tonight they shared the same watch at the gate. Nisus said: "Euryalus — is it the gods who put this fire in us, or does each man make a god of his own fierce wanting? Something has been driving me, a long time now, to throw myself into a fight, into some great thing — I can't sit still and rest. You see how sure of themselves the Rutulians are. Their fires are scattered and low; they're sprawled out drunk and asleep; the whole place is quiet. Listen — here's what I've been turning over. Everyone, the soldiers and the council both, wants Aeneas brought back, wants men sent to carry him word. If they'll promise you what I'm about to ask for myself — for me the glory of it is reward enough — then I think, down at the foot of that hill, I can find a way through to the walls of Pallanteum, where Aeneas is."

Euryalus was struck through with a great love of glory, and he answered his eager friend: "And you'd leave me out of this — send you off alone into the worst of it? Is that what you think of me? No. That isn't how my father Opheltes raised me, in the thick of the wars at Troy and the terror of the Greeks. That isn't how I've borne myself at your side, following Aeneas and his fate to the last. There's a heart in me that holds the daylight cheap and would think a life well spent to buy the honor you're after." Nisus said: "I never doubted you — I couldn't. So may great Jupiter, or whatever god looks kindly on this, bring me back to you in triumph. But if something goes wrong — and you can see how much can go wrong in a thing like this — if some chance or some god drags me down, I want you to outlive me. You're younger; you deserve more of life than I do. Let there be someone to carry my body out of the fight, or to ransom it back, and lay it in the ground; or, if luck even denies that, to make the offerings to an empty tomb and keep my name. And I won't be the cause of such grief to your poor mother, the one woman of all of them brave enough to follow you here, who wouldn't stay behind safe in Acestes' city." But Euryalus answered: "You're spinning out reasons that don't hold. My mind's made up and it won't change. Let's go — now." And he shook the sleeping guards awake to take their places. Then the two of them left their post and went to find Ascanius.

Every other living thing on earth had let its cares go and lay easy in sleep. But the chief men of Troy, the pick of them, were holding a council under arms about the desperate state of things — should they take up weapons, who could carry word to Aeneas. They stood there in the middle of the camp leaning on their long spears, shields on their arms. And into the middle of them came Nisus and Euryalus, in a hurry, begging to be let in: it was urgent, they said, worth the interruption. Ascanius welcomed the two flushed boys and told Nisus to speak. So the son of Hyrtacus said: "Men of Aeneas — hear us out, and don't judge what we're offering by our years. The Rutulians have drunk themselves into sleep; their fires are dying. We've spotted a gap for ourselves, where the road forks at the gate down by the sea. Their fires are broken there, the smoke is rolling up black. Give us the chance, and we'll make our way to Aeneas and the walls of Pallanteum, and you'll see him back here soon, loaded with the spoils of a great slaughter. There's no fear of losing the road. We've hunted that valley in the dim light over and over; we've seen the first of the city's roofs from there, and we know the whole river, every ford of it."

Then old Aletes, heavy with years and ripe in judgment, spoke: "Gods of our fathers — Troy is never wholly abandoned while you raise up young men with hearts like these." And as he said it the tears ran down, and he caught both of them by the shoulders and the hands. "What reward could match what you two are giving? The finest the gods will pay, and your own good conscience. The rest, dutiful Aeneas will give you with his own hands, the moment he's back; and so will Ascanius, who'll never forget a service like this as long as he lives." "No," said Ascanius — "my whole hope hangs on my father's safe return. I swear to you both, Nisus, by our household gods, by the great Penates of Assaracus, by the hearth of white-haired Vesta: everything I have, every hope I hold, I put in your hands. Bring my father back to me. Let me see his face again, and nothing else matters. I'll give you two cups worked in silver, embossed with figures, that my father took at the sack of Arisba; two tripods; two great talents of gold; and an old wine-bowl that Dido of Sidon gave me. And if we win Italy and take the throne and divide the spoils — you saw the horse Turnus rides, his gold armor, his crest? That horse, Nisus, and the shield, and the blood-red crest — I'll set them apart now: they're already yours, your prize. And my father will give you twelve chosen women and twelve captive men, all with their own armor, and besides that, all the land King Latinus himself holds. As for you, dear boy, whose years are closer to my own — I take you to my heart here and now, for everything that's coming. There's no glory of mine I won't share with you. War or peace, I'll trust my deepest counsel and my whole faith to you."

Euryalus answered him: "No day will ever find me unequal to a thing this brave — only let fortune fall my way and not against me. But there's one gift I'll ask, past all the rest. I have a mother, of Priam's ancient line, and the poor woman couldn't be kept from following me — not by the land of Troy, not by King Acestes' walls. I'm leaving her now without a word, without the blessing of a goodbye — I swear it by the night and by your right hand — because I couldn't bear her tears. So you be a comfort to her, I beg you. Stand in for me when she's left helpless. Let me carry that hope away with me, and I'll go braver into anything." The hearts of the Trojans broke at that, and the tears came — Ascanius most of all, the picture of a son's love going straight through him. And he said: "I promise you everything your great venture deserves. Your mother will be my mother — she'll lack nothing but the name Creusa — and a son like you has earned her no small honor, whatever comes of this. By my own head I swear it, the oath my father swore: whatever I promised you if you come back and it all goes well, the same will go to your mother and your house." And weeping as he spoke, he took the gold-mounted sword from his own shoulder — a wonder of craft, the work of Lycaon of Cnossos, sheathed in fitted ivory — and gave it to Euryalus. Mnestheus gave Nisus a lion's shaggy hide; loyal old Aletes traded helmets with him. So armed, they went, and the whole company of the Trojan leaders, young and old, walked them to the gate with their prayers — Ascanius above all, a man before his time, his heart already a grown man's, loading them with messages for his father. But all of it the winds tore loose and scattered to the empty clouds.

They crossed the ditch, and went out through the shadows toward the enemy camp — bound to be the death of many before their own night ended. They found the Rutulians stretched out drunk and asleep all over the grass, the chariots tipped up empty on the shore, the men sprawled among the reins and the wheels, wine-cups lying where they'd dropped. Nisus spoke first: "Euryalus — now's the time to use our hands. The road's open. You keep watch behind me; look out, all around, that no one comes up at our backs. I'll clear the way ahead and cut you a wide path through them." He said it under his breath, and then he went at proud Rhamnes with his sword. Rhamnes lay there propped high on his heaped rugs, breathing deep in his sleep — a king, and Turnus's own favorite seer; but no skill at prophecy could ward off death. Three of his servants lay sprawled nearby among the weapons, and Nisus killed them, and the squire too, and the charioteer caught under the horses' feet, and lopped their lolling heads off. Then their master Remus — he cut the head clean from his shoulders and left the trunk pumping, the warm black blood soaking the bedding and the ground. He killed Lamyrus and Lamus and young Serranus, a beautiful boy who'd gambled late into the night and now lay overcome by the god of wine — happy, if he'd kept the dice going till dawn. He went through them like a starving lion turned loose in a crowded fold, mad with hunger, mauling and dragging the soft helpless flock that bleats and dies under its jaws, his mouth running blood.

And Euryalus was killing too, no less, blazing with it, mowing down the nameless crowd as he came on — Fadus, Herbesus, Rhoetus, Abaris, all caught unawares. Rhoetus was awake, watching it all; he tried to hide behind a great wine-bowl, but as he rose Euryalus drove the whole length of the blade into his chest and pulled it out red. He spat up his life in a flood of dark blood and wine, dying where he lay. And Euryalus pressed on, hot with the killing. He was nearly at Messapus's men now, where the last fires were guttering and the war-horses stood tethered, cropping the grass — when Nisus saw how far the lust for slaughter was carrying them both, and pulled him up short: "Enough. The light's coming, and the light is no friend to us. We've cut our lane through them; we've had our blood. Let's stop here." They left behind a fortune in arms, in solid silver, in worked bronze and rich rugs. But Euryalus couldn't resist Rhamnes's gear — the gold studs of the sword-belt; and he caught up Messapus's helmet too, light and crested, and slung the belt over his shoulder. Then they slipped out of the camp and made for safe ground.

But meanwhile a column of cavalry had been sent ahead from the Latin city while the main army waited on the plain — three hundred horsemen, all carrying shields, with Volcens at their head, riding to bring Turnus an answer. They were close to the camp now, nearing the walls, when they caught sight of the two friends slipping off down a fork in the road to the left — and there, in the half-light of the early dawn, Euryalus's stolen helmet betrayed him, the moon catching it and throwing it back, the one thing he'd forgotten. It didn't pass unnoticed. "Halt! You there — who are you?" Volcens shouted from the column. "Why under arms? Where are you going? Whose men?" The two said nothing; they bolted for the woods and put their trust in the dark. But the horsemen scattered to block the known paths and threw a ring of guards around every way out. The forest was a wide tangle of black underbrush and bristling holm-oak, choked everywhere with dense thornbushes; here and there a faint track glimmered through the broken ground. Euryalus, slowed by the dark of the branches and the weight of his plunder, lost his bearings and missed the path in his fear. Nisus got clear; he'd already run past the enemy and the place that later took its name from Alba, where King Latinus then kept his high cattle-pens — when he stopped, and looked back for his friend, and his friend wasn't there. "Euryalus," he cried, "poor boy — where did I lose you? Which way? Where?" And he turned, and ran back the whole tangled length of the wood, retracing his own steps, hunting through the silent thickets.

He heard horses, then the noise of pursuit, then the signal-calls. And a moment later a shout reached him — and there was Euryalus. The whole troop had him; the dark and the strange ground had betrayed him, and they'd swept down and dragged him off, struggling, helpless. What could Nisus do? What weapon, what strength could tear the boy loose? Should he just throw himself into their swords and die, and make his death glorious with wounds? He drew his arm back fast, lifted his eyes to the high moon, and prayed: "You, goddess — you, glory of the stars, watcher over the woods, Latona's daughter — help me now. If my father Hyrtacus ever brought offerings to your altars for my sake, if I ever added to them from my own hunting, hung your dome with spoils or nailed them to your sacred eaves — let me throw this crowd into chaos. Steady my hand." He finished, and threw, putting his whole body behind the spear. The shaft flew hissing through the shadows of the night and drove into Sulmo's back, snapped off, and the splintered wood went on through his heart. He rolled over, vomiting a hot stream of blood from his chest, his sides heaving in long spasms, and died. The riders looked wildly around. And Nisus, fiercer now, was already balancing a second spear by his ear — and while they were still in confusion it went whistling clean through both of Tagus's temples and stuck there, warm, in the pierced brain.

Volcens was wild with rage, and could find no one to take it out on — no sign of who had thrown — nowhere to aim his fury. "You'll pay for both of them, then," he said, "with your own warm blood," and went for Euryalus with his sword drawn. Then Nisus lost his mind with terror — he couldn't stay hidden, couldn't hold himself back, couldn't bear that much grief. He burst out into the open shouting: "Me — me — I'm here, I did it, turn your swords on me, Rutulians! It was all mine, the whole thing. He didn't dare, he couldn't have — I swear it by the sky and the stars that know — all he was guilty of was loving his luckless friend too much." But the words came too late: the sword was already driven home, hard, and it tore through the boy's white ribs. Euryalus rolled in death, the blood streaming down his lovely body, his neck sinking limp on his shoulder — the way a bright flower cut by the plow droops and dies, or poppies bow their heads on tired stalks when the rain has caught them and weighed them down. But Nisus went straight into the thick of them, going for Volcens alone, only Volcens. They closed around him, beat him back, hacked at him from every side; he kept driving on, whirling his sword like lightning, until he buried it full in the Rutulian's open, shouting mouth, and killed the man as his own life went out of him. Then, riddled through, he threw himself down on his dead friend's body, and there at last found his rest in death.

Fortunate pair! If my verse has any power, no day will ever erase you from the memory of time — not while the house of Aeneas keeps its place by the Capitol's unshaken rock, not while a Roman father rules the empire of the world.

The Rutulians, the winners of the field, took their spoils and their losses both — and carried their dead commander Volcens, weeping, back to the camp. And there the grief grew, for they found Rhamnes dead, and so many of their chiefs cut down in one slaughter — Serranus, Numa, all of them. Crowds gathered around the bodies and the dying, around the ground still warm and steaming with fresh blood and the runnels of it. And they knew Messapus's gleaming helmet among the spoils, and the war-gear, all of it won back at a bitter cost.

By now Dawn was rising from Tithonus's saffron bed, sowing the first light over the earth. The sun came up and stripped the world of shadow, and Turnus, fully armed, called his men to arms, and each captain led his bristling lines out for the fight, and whetted their anger with the news. And — a sight to make the eyes shrink from it — they fixed the heads of Nisus and Euryalus on the points of two spears and carried them out high, with a great shout behind them. The hardened Trojans manned the left wall to face it — the right was covered by the river — and held the wide ditches and stood in their towers, grieving, because they knew the faces lifted up there, all too well, even smeared and dripping with dark gore. And rumor flew on its quick wings through the frightened camp and slid into the ears of Euryalus's mother. In a heartbeat the warmth went out of the poor woman's body. The shuttle dropped from her hand and the thread unspooled. She ran out wailing, tearing her hair the way women do in grief, and rushed straight for the walls and the front ranks, careless of the men, careless of the danger, the spears, and filled the sky with her keening:

"Is this you, Euryalus? Is this how I see you — you, the late comfort of my old age? Cruel boy, how could you leave me alone? They sent you into such danger, and they didn't even let your poor mother say goodbye. Now you lie in a strange land, food for the dogs and the carrion-birds of Latium, and I — your mother — I never walked behind your bier, never closed your eyes, never washed your wounds, never wrapped you in the cloak I sat weaving day and night, all those nights, easing my old age with the work. Where do I even go? What ground holds your torn body now, your hacked limbs, your remains? Is this all you've brought back to me, my son — this? Is this what I followed you over land and sea for? Run me through, Rutulians, if you have any pity. Throw all your spears at me. Kill me first. Or you, great father of the gods, take pity, and hurl my hated life down to the underworld with your bolt, since there's no other way I can break off this cruel living." Her wailing went through them and broke their spirit; a groan of sorrow ran the length of the ranks; their fighting edge went numb and dull. And while she was still feeding the fire of grief, Idaeus and Actor, at Ilioneus's word and the word of Ascanius, who was weeping hard, took her up between them and carried her back inside.

Then, from far off, the brazen trumpet rang its terrible song. A shout went up behind it, and the sky echoed it back. The Volscians came on under a roof of locked shields, racing in to fill the ditches and tear down the palisade. Some looked for a way over the wall, where the defenders stood thin and the ring of men showed gaps. The Trojans rained everything down on them — they'd learned in ten years of war how to defend a wall — pikes and missiles of every kind, and rolled heavy stakes down to break the shield-roof, though the men under it took the punishment grimly, packed shoulder to shoulder. But it couldn't hold. Where the enemy massed thickest, the Trojans heaved over a great boulder that crushed a wide lane through them and cracked the shield-roof open, and the brave Rutulians lost their appetite for fighting blind under cover, and fell back to clearing the ramparts with their spears from a distance instead.

Elsewhere, the grim Mezentius shook a smoking Etruscan pine-brand and flung fire. And Messapus, the tamer of horses, son of Neptune, ripped through the stockade and shouted for ladders to scale the wall. I call on you now, Calliope, and all the Muses, to help me sing the slaughter Turnus dealt that day, the men he sent down to death, each warrior felled — unroll with me the great scroll of the war. You remember it, goddesses; you have the power to tell it.

There was a tower, high and commanding, with bridges running up to it — set in a strong spot, and every Italian strained to storm it, every Trojan strained with all his strength to hold it, hurling stones and pouring spears out through the loopholes packed inside. Turnus opened it: he flung a torch and the flame caught the side of it. Driven by the wind, it ran up the planks and gnawed at the gateways where it bit in. Inside, the men panicked, crowded together, tried to fall back from the fire — and as they bunched to the one side that hadn't caught, the weight tipped the whole tower, and it came down with a crash that shook the sky, the men falling with it to the earth, the great mass on top of them, run through by their own weapons, their chests staked on the splintered beams. Only two broke free, Helenor and Lycus. Helenor was the elder, a son the Lydian king had secretly fathered on the slave Licymnia and sent to Troy against the rules, lightly armed — a plain sword, a white shield with no device on it. When he found himself ringed by Turnus's thousands, lines of the enemy thick on every side, he did what a wild beast does when the hunters have it boxed in — he threw himself, savage, straight onto their spears, choosing the death he knew was coming, and leaping toward the place the steel ran thickest. But Lycus, faster on his feet, dodged through the enemy and the weapons and made the wall, straining to grab the top of it and the hands of his friends reaching down. Turnus had chased him the whole way, spear and voice both, and now he taunted him: "Did you really think you'd slip away from me, you fool?" — and caught him as he dangled and tore him down, ripping away a chunk of the wall with him. He was like the eagle of Jupiter snatching a hare or a white swan up into the sky in its hooked talons, or the wolf of Mars pulling a lamb from the fold while its mother bleats and bleats for it. The shout went up on every side. The Rutulians rushed the ditches, filling them, and flung firebrands up onto the high roofs.

Ilioneus brought down Lucetius with a mountain of broken rock as he came at the gate with fire. Liger killed Emathion, Asilas killed Corynaeus — one the better archer, the other deadly with a hidden spear thrown from far off. Caeneus killed Ortygius; Turnus killed the victor Caeneus, and then Itys, and Clonius, and Dioxippus, and Promolus, and Sagaris, and Idas standing high on the towers. Capys killed Privernus — Themillas's spear had grazed him first, and the fool dropped his shield to clap a hand over the wound, and the arrow came in and pinned the hand to his left side and burst the breath out of his lungs deep in his chest. The son of Arcens stood out among them, in beautiful armor, his cloak embroidered and dyed bright Spanish purple, a striking boy — his father had raised him in the grove of Mars by the streams of the Symaethus, where the rich, gentle altar of Palicus stands. Mezentius set down his spear, took up the sling, whirled the thong three times around his head, and let fly: the lead split the boy's skull straight down the middle and stretched him out full-length in the sand.

That was the day Ascanius — who till then had only ever bent his bow at fleeing game in the woods — first let an arrow fly in war, and brought down a fighting man. He killed bold Numanus, called Remulus, who had lately married Turnus's younger sister. Numanus had been strutting up and down in front of the lines, swollen with his new royal kinship, bellowing things fit and unfit to say, full of himself: "Aren't you ashamed, you twice-captured Phrygians, penned up behind a wall a second time, holding ditches between yourselves and death? And these are the men who came to take our women by war! What god, what madness drove you to Italy? You'll find no sons of Atreus here, no smooth-tongued Ulysses spinning lies.
