We're a tough race from a hard root. We carry our newborn sons straight to the river and break them in on the cold of it. Our boys go without sleep to hunt the forests; their sport is to ride down game and bend the bow. Our young men take hard work without flinching, lean on little; they tame the soil with the harrow or shake towns loose in battle. Iron wears at us our whole lives long — we turn the goad around and prod the oxen with the butt of the spear. Slow old age doesn't weaken the spirit in us or sap our strength. We press the helmet down over our gray hair, and we still love to haul home fresh plunder and live off what we take. But you — you wear saffron and gleaming purple, embroidered; you live for lying around; you love to dance. Your tunics have sleeves; your bonnets have ribbons. Phrygian women, that's what you are — not Phrygian men! Go play on the heights of Dindyma, where the pipe sings its double notes for ears like yours. The drums are calling you, the boxwood flute of the Mother of Ida. Leave the weapons to men."

Ascanius could not stand to hear such filth, such an evil omen of a boast. He drew the gut taut across an arrow, faced the man, spread his arms wide to bend the bow — and first stopped to pray, with a vow: "Almighty Jupiter, bless what I'm about to dare. I'll bring my own gifts to your temple every year. I'll lead a snow-white bullock to your altar, its horns gilded, head already as high as its mother's, butting and pawing the sand." The Father heard, and thundered on the left out of a clear sky, and in the same instant the deadly bow twanged. The arrow went whistling out, drove straight through Numanus's head, and split both temples open. "Go on," said Ascanius — "mock real courage with your big words. This is the answer the twice-captured Phrygians send back to the Rutulians." That was all he said; but the Trojans took it up with a roar of joy, lifting their hearts to the stars.

And from a cloud high overhead Apollo happened to be watching the Italian lines and the city, and he spoke to the victorious boy: "Blessings on your new courage, boy — that's the road to the stars. Born of gods, you will father gods. All the wars that are fated to come will rightly end under the house of Assaracus; Troy is too small to hold you." And with that the god came down out of the sky, parting the air, and went to find Ascanius. He put on the look of old Butes, who had once been Anchises's armor-bearer and faithful gatekeeper, and whom Aeneas had since set over his son — the wrinkled face, the voice, the gray hair, the grim old soldier's bearing and weapons. He spoke to the boy, whose blood was up: "Son of Aeneas — let it be enough that Numanus fell to your arrow and you took no hurt. Great Apollo grants you this first glory and doesn't grudge a marksman his equal. But now, boy, hold back from the war." And in the middle of his words Apollo left them and vanished out of their sight into the thin air. The Trojan captains knew the god by his weapons, and heard the rattle of his quiver as he went, and so by Apollo's will and word they held Ascanius back from the fighting, eager as he was for glory; and they themselves went back into the danger, where life hung on every blow.

The shout ran the whole length of the walls and the towers. They bent their savage bows; they whirled the sling-thongs. The ground was carpeted with spent shafts, and helmets and hollow shields rang under the blows — the battle swelling like a rainstorm driven up out of the west when the rainy Kids are rising, like hail rattling onto the sea when Jupiter wheels his black squalls in off the south and the storm-clouds split open in the sky.

Now Pandarus and Bitias, sons of Alcanor of Ida, raised in Jupiter's grove by the woodland nymph Iaera — two giants, tall as the firs and the mountains that bore them — threw open the gate their commander had ordered them to keep shut, and dared the enemy to come in. Trusting their own strength, they stood inside on the left and right like two armed towers, the steel flashing on them, the crests tossing high over their heads — the way two oaks lift their leafy crowns to the sky on the banks of the Po or beside lovely Athesis, swaying their unshorn tops and nodding to each other in the wind. In poured the Rutulians the moment they saw the gate standing open. At once Quercens, and Aquiculus in his fine armor, and headlong Tmarus, and Haemon, son of Mars, were either thrown back with their whole troop, or died right there in the throat of the gate. The fury rose hotter on both sides; and now the Trojans came pouring out where the Rutulians were thickest and dared to fight them hand to hand in the open in front of the gate.

Turnus was raging in another part of the field, scattering the Trojans, when word reached him that the enemy was hot with fresh slaughter and had thrown his own men open to the gates. He broke off, and ran in white heat for the gate and the two arrogant brothers. The first to fall was Antiphates — Sarpedon's bastard son by a Theban woman — Turnus's spear caught him first; the Italian cornel-wood flew through the soft air, drove into his belly and high into his chest, and the dark wound brought up a foaming gush of blood, the iron warm in the pierced lung. Then he killed Meropes, and Erymas, and Aphidnus; and then Bitias, his eyes blazing, his blood up — not with a spear, no spear would have stopped a man that size, but a whirling lance, a great javelin that came roaring in like a thunderbolt. Two bull-hides couldn't turn it, and the trusty corselet with its double scales of gold couldn't turn it; the huge body buckled and went down. The earth groaned under it, and the great shield clashed down on top of him. So a stone pier collapses on the shore at Baiae — the kind they build of massive blocks and sink in the sea — dragged down all at once, smashing into the shallows, the water boiling up black and the sand churned to the surface, so that the island of Prochyta shakes with the noise of it, and Ischia, the hard bed laid on Typhoeus by Jupiter's command.

Now Mars, lord of war, breathed strength and fight into the Latins and stung them deep, and loosed Flight and dark Panic among the Trojans. The Latins came on from every side, the war-god in their hearts at last. When Pandarus saw his brother dead, and how the day was turning, how far the luck had run against them, he put his shoulder to the gate and swung it shut on its hinges with all his weight — and so he locked many of his own men out, abandoned to the enemy in the brutal fight; but others, fool that he was, he shut inside with him, and he never saw Turnus among them, never saw he had penned the king of the Rutulians up inside the walls, loose among them like a monstrous tiger turned in among a defenseless flock. A strange new light flared in Turnus's eyes; his armor clashed and rang; the blood-red crest shook on his helmet; and his shield threw off a blinding glare. The Trojans knew that hated face and the huge frame, and panic took them. But Pandarus came charging out, on fire with rage at his brother's death, and shouted: "This is no dowry-palace of Queen Amata's; this is no walled Ardea that takes Turnus in to his home country. You're looking at an enemy camp. There's no way out of here." Turnus said, calmly, smiling: "Then start it, if you've got the heart. Come on. You can tell Priam, when you meet him down there, that you found Achilles here too." Pandarus put his whole strength behind a rough spear, knots and bark and all — but the air took it; Juno turned the flying point aside, and it stuck fast in the gate. "This one you won't dodge," said Turnus. "My hand is stronger, and my blade." And he rose to his full height, his sword high overhead, and brought it straight down through the middle of the brow, splitting the smooth young face clean in two between the cheeks, a terrible wound. The earth shook with the crash of the great body falling; the dying limbs sprawled out, the armor splashed with brains and blood, and the head hung in two even halves, one on each shoulder.

The Trojans scattered in terror. And if Turnus had only thought, right then, to break the bars and let his comrades in through the gate, that day would have been the last of the war and the last of the Trojans. But the blind lust of slaughter drove him on, raging after the men in front of him. He hamstrung Phaleris; he cut Gyges down; he snatched up their spears and threw them into the backs of the fleeing Trojans, Juno feeding him strength and courage. He sent Halys after them, and Phegeus with his shield run through, and then — caught off guard up on the walls, still shouting their war-cries — Alcander and Halius and Noëmon and Prytanis. Lynceus came at him, calling his men on, and Turnus, swinging from the right, met him with one stroke of the sword that took the head clean off, helmet and all, at sword's length. Then he killed Amycus, the slaughterer of wild game, the best hand alive at smearing iron with poison; and Clytius, son of Aeolus; and Cretheus, the Muses' friend, Cretheus their companion, who'd always loved a song and a lyre and the run of his fingers over the strings, and was forever singing of horses and weapons and men and wars.

At last the Trojan captains, Mnestheus and fierce Serestus, heard of the carnage and came running, and saw their men scattered and the enemy inside the walls. Mnestheus rounded on them: "Where do you think you're running to? Where? What other walls do you have left, beyond these? Men — one man, fenced in on every side by your own ramparts, has poured all this blood through the camp, sent all your best young men down to death — and not one of you ashamed of it, not one of you pitying his poor country, the old gods, the great Aeneas?" That fired them. They steadied, drew together, and stood. And Turnus began to give ground, little by little, edging toward the part of the camp the river ringed. The Trojans came after him all the harder, roaring, massing — the way a crowd closes in on a fierce lion, hedging it with spears, and the beast, frightened now but still savage, glaring, backs off slowly, too proud and too furious to turn and run, but unable to force a way through the men and the weapons, much as it longs to. Just so Turnus drew back, unhurried, doubtful, the anger boiling in him. Even then he charged the thick of them twice, twice sent them flying in a panic the length of the walls. But the whole camp was massing against him now, and not even Juno, daughter of Saturn, dared keep feeding him strength against them all, because Jupiter sent Iris down out of the sky with hard orders for his sister: Turnus must leave the Trojan walls.

So now the young man could no longer hold his own — not with his shield, not with his sword-arm — buried under the storm of weapons coming at him from every side. The helmet rang and rang around his hollow temples; the solid bronze split open under the stones; the crest was beaten flat off his head; the shield-boss could not take the blows. The Trojans, Mnestheus at their head like a thunderbolt, doubled their spears. The sweat ran down Turnus's whole body in a black river; he had no breath left; a sick exhaustion shook his shattered frame. Then at last, armor and all, he threw himself headlong into the river. The Tiber took him in its tawny flood as he fell, lifted him gently on its waves, washed the blood off him, and gave him back, glad of it, to his own.

sections.label: Book X
sections.title: The Council of the Gods, the Death of Pallas, and the End of Mezentius

segments.text: Meanwhile the house of almighty Olympus swung open, and the father of gods and king of men called a council in his starry hall. From his high seat he looked down over the whole earth — the Trojan camp, the Latin lines, the war and all its turns. The gods took their places in order, the great and the lesser, and he began: "Powers of heaven — why has it all turned back on itself? Why these murmurs, this change of heart? I forbade Italy to go to war with the Trojans. What is this quarrel, then, against my command? What fear has driven the one side or the other to take up arms? The right time for war will come — don't rush it on. The day will come when fierce Carthage opens the Alps and pours destruction down on the strongholds of Rome. Then you can hate, then you can take sides, then you can tear each other apart for it. For now, leave it alone. Settle your hearts, and keep the peace I set."

Jupiter said it in few words. But golden Venus answered him at length: "Father — eternal power, where else can we turn for help? Look at the Rutulians, swaggering across the field unpunished. Look at Turnus, riding high through his ranks in his shining armor, sure of himself. The Trojans can't even hold their own walls now; the camp is choked with slaughter, the trenches running red. And Aeneas is far off, knowing none of it, his men left exposed with no one to lead them. Is this to go on? Is Troy to be stormed and burned a second time, a new army at her gates, a new Diomedes risen against her? I, your daughter, am bracing for one more wound. If my people came to Italy against your will, without your leave, then let them pay for breaking the law — take your hand from them, I won't ask you to save them. But if they came following all the oracles heaven and the dead alike gave them, who has the right now to overturn your word and write another fate? Need I remind you of the storm at sea, of Aeolus loosed against Neptune's own waters? Of Iris sent down to drive the Trojan women mad and burn the fleet? And now Juno has gone down to the underworld itself — that was the one outrage left to try — and stirred up the Fury Allecto to madden the quiet hearts of the Latin women. I don't care about empire anymore. I hoped for it once, while heaven was still kind. Let those you favor win. But I beg you one thing, father — if I may still call you that — by Troy in her ashes: let Ascanius be drawn out of this war and live. Let the father be cast where fate will, but spare the boy. Cythera is mine; the towers of Cyprus are mine. Let him lay his weapons down there, out of the light, with no crown and no claim, and let Carthage trample Italy unafraid. What good did it do my son to escape the fire, to carry his gods and his father out through the flames, to cross all those seas, only to raise a second Troy and watch it fall too?"

Then royal Juno, swelling with deep anger, broke in: "Must I say out loud what should have stayed decently silent — what I'd have kept to myself, if you hadn't forced it with this slander? Did any god or any man tell your darling Aeneas to fall on the Latins by surprise and start a war? Fate brought him, you'll say, and the will of the gods. Say the truth, then — it was mad Cassandra he listened to, not heaven. Did I send him off to leave his half-built second Troy to a beardless boy and go wandering the waves again? Did I tell him to go begging the Etruscans for help and arm a country that wanted peace? Did Iris give that advice, or I? You think it monstrous that Latins should defend their own soil with fire and sword. But it's perfectly fair, is it, for foreigners to seize land that isn't theirs, to carry off another man's promised bride, to sue for peace with one hand while they arm with the other? You were allowed to pull your son out of the fight — to draw the coward back from danger and leave a hollow phantom in his place. You turned the fire from the burning ships and changed the hulls into sea-nymphs. But let me lift one finger to help my own, and that's a crime? You say your son is absent, knowing nothing of what his enemies are planning. Then let him stay absent. Cythera is yours, you said, and the towers of Cyprus and the soft retreats. Why come stirring up a warlike people, then? Did I burn down Troy, or you? Who let loose the disaster — me, or the man whose lust began the whole war? Remember whose word the adulterer trusted; remember who promised him the Spartan queen. When all of Greece banded together to wipe out that treacherous breed — that was the time to fear for Troy. Now your grief and your complaints come too late."

So Juno spoke, and a murmur ran through the gods, some for her, some against — like the first stir of winds still trapped in the woods, trying out their voices in whispers before they break loose onto the open sea and roar a storm at the trembling sailors. Then the almighty Father, who shakes heaven on its hinges with a nod, answered them both. When he speaks, the whole assembly stands still and listens; the clouds break apart, the winds hold their breath, the waves lie down flat. "Hear me, then, and take it to heart. Since the Trojans and the Latins cannot be joined in the alliance I wanted, and since your endless quarreling only ruins the peace of heaven — from this hour I leave the war to fate. Let each man stand or fall by his own fortune. Rutulian or Trojan, I make no difference between them; I look on all of them with the same eye. Whether it's the camp's defenders who are held in by fate or the Trojans' own blunders, I'll favor neither. Let each side find the lot fate deals it. Jupiter is king over all alike; the Fates will find their way." And he sealed it by the river of his brother's kingdom, by the banks of pitch and the black torrent of Styx, and bent his head — and all of Olympus shook at the nod. That ended the council. Jupiter rose from his golden throne, and the gods gathered round and walked him back to his halls.

Meanwhile the Rutulians pressed their siege on every gate, cutting men down, setting fires, hemming the Trojan army in behind its own walls. The defenders stood thin on the towers, longing in vain for their absent commander, with no hope of escape and less hope of relief. Still, some of them held the line in the face of it: Asius and the brave brothers of Sarpedon's blood, both the Assaraci, young Haemon who was ready to die young, Clarus and Thymoetes, Tibris and Castor of Lycia. From Acmon's hands came a stone so huge it half deserved to be called a mountain; he was a big-boned, hard-sinewed youth, as strong as his brother Mnestheus or as Aeneas's own father. Some hurled firebrands, some loosed flights of arrows, some fought with spears, some with stones. And there in the thick of it stood the beautiful boy — Ascanius, the care of Venus and the hope of Troy. His head was bare, his lovely face uncovered, his hair falling in curls over his shoulders, a band of gold around his brow; he stood out among the rest like a gem set in gold against dark jet.

So the deadly war was waged on both sides. And all that while Aeneas was cutting through the night on the open sea. For when he left Evander, he had gone to the Etruscan camp and the tent of King Tarchon, told him his name and his country, asked for help, laid out the terms — his own slim strength, the vengeance proud Mezentius was preparing, and Turnus's headlong fury. He reminded Tarchon how uncertain human fortune is, and mixed his warning with a plea. Tarchon signed the treaty without delay and joined his Etruscan forces to the Trojans. So the fleet set sail, fate no longer holding it back, their cause now trusted to a foreign hand. Aeneas led the way. On his stern stood two carved lions of Mount Ida — Ida, forever dear to the wandering Trojans. Under the figurehead's shade he sat, turning the war over in his mind, the changing chances of it. At his left side young Pallas kept close, asking him now about the winds, now about the stars and the dark sea-road, now about all he had borne by land and water.

Open your fountains now, you Muses — sing the Etruscan captains and their host, the men who followed great Aeneas to war. Tell their arms, their numbers, their names. First Massicus, riding the Tiger over the foaming sea, leading a thousand men he had brought from Asium and from Cosa — armed with light quivers, bows, and arrows. Next fierce Abas, his men in bright bronze, a gilded statue of Apollo on his stern; Populonia had sent him six hundred soldiers trained for war, and the island of Ilva three hundred more, an island rich in iron from its bottomless mines. Third came Asilas, the man who reads heaven and the wandering stars, who finds omens in the entrails of victims and in the rolling thunder — a thousand spears stood under his command, sent by the people of Pisa. After him fair Astur, proud of his fine horse and his painted shield: Caere and the fens of Gravisca sent him three hundred, with the men of Minio's fields and of Pyrgi, all bred to arms.

And you, Muse — bring back the name of Cinyras, and brave Cupavo with his few followers, whose helmet wore the swan's plumes that told his family's story. For his father Cycnus, grieving for the loss of Phaeton he had loved, sang his sorrow in the poplar groves under the shade of the mourning Sisters, until heaven turned his gray hair to soft white feathers and lifted him into the air, singing as he flew. His son Cupavo now swept the salt water, a Centaur carved on his stern, heaving a great rock as if to hurl it, threatening the sea below. Next came Ocnus, leading his own men, son of the prophetess Manto and the Tuscan river, who gave Mantua its name — an ancient town of mixed blood, three tribes in it, four peoples under each tribe, all of them ruled by Mantua and her Etruscan law. And hatred of Mezentius had armed five hundred more under Mincius — son of Lake Benacus, his brow crowned with gray reeds — led by grave Auletes, his hundred oars sweeping the glassy deep all at once. The sea-green Triton bore him, frowning on his prow, blowing his curved conch shell so the waves danced at the blast: hairy and human above the waist, a great fish below, the surf foaming white where his breast cut the water. So thirty chosen ships drove on across the brine, bearing relief to Troy.

Now the sun had left the world, and gentle Phoebe was halfway through her night-ride across the sky. Aeneas, who never closed his eyes, sat at the helm himself, tending the rudder and the sails. And midway over the sea a chorus of sea-nymphs met him — his own ships, once cut from the wood of Ida, now changed into as many maidens of the deep, swimming where the tall hulls had ridden. They knew him from far off, and ringed his vessel round. Cymodoce, whose voice was clearest of them all, came up behind, laid her right hand on the stern, lifted her white breast above the waves, and rowed with her left through the curling water. She spoke for the whole chorus to the man who knew nothing of it: "Are you asleep, son of the goddess? Wake — and crowd on all your sail, and drive your course! We are your fleet, the pines of Ida, now nymphs of the sea. When Turnus came at us with fire and sword while we lay at anchor, we broke our cables — much against our will, to leave our master — and we have been searching the Etruscan deep for you ever since. The great Mother had pity and gave us these shapes and a deathless life in the water. But your son Ascanius is hard pressed inside his walls, ringed by the ditches and the spears of the Latins. The Arcadian horse and the Etruscans are already in their places. Turnus means to throw his squadrons across their road and cut them off before they reach the Trojan lines. So rise — and when the rose of dawn breaks, call your men to arms first of all. Take up the unbreakable shield the fire-god forged for you. Tomorrow's sun, unless my skill is empty, will look down on great heaps of the enemy slain." She finished, and as she dove she pushed the hull forward with a deathless strength — she knew the sea-road well — and the ship shot ahead faster than the wind. The rest of the fleet caught up. Aeneas, not knowing the reason, marveled at the speed of it, and took heart from the omen.

Then he prayed, lifting his eyes to heaven: "Great Mother of the gods, crowned with towers, queen of Ida where the leashed tigers obey you — confirm your own omens for me. Lead us into the fight, and let your Trojans win under your hand." That was all. And now the new day had chased the shadows off. He gave the order: the men were to follow the standards, ready their weapons, and steel themselves for the war that was coming. Then, from his high stern, he caught sight of his camp below, ringed by the enemy — and he raised his blazing shield in his left hand and held it high. The Trojans on the walls saw the sign and roared back, every voice at once, their hope kindled fresh; from the towers they let their spears fly with doubled force, like cranes against a dark southern storm, blackening the whole sky as they came on. King Turnus and his captains wondered at the fighting flaring up again — until they looked back, and saw the sea covered with sails and the swift ships running for the shore. The Latins stared with dazzled eyes at the crest on Aeneas's helmet, a flame seeming to rise from his head and pour fire across the field, and the keen glitter of the golden shield — the way a comet burns blood-red in the night and saddens the sky, or the dog-star Sirius flashes its sickly light and brings disease and drought to frighten mankind.

But Turnus's nerve never failed. He set himself to hold the beach and keep the Trojans from landing, and he fired his men's hearts: "What you've prayed for so long, kind fortune hands you now — to meet the enemy with weapons in your hands. The day is yours. Only dare it, and your swords will win the war. Each of you, remember your fathers, your sons, your homes, your fields, your wives — all of it is in your hands today. Live up to the men you came from; match your fathers' fame in arms. Hit them now, while they're still staggering up the strand on unsteady feet. Fortune favors the bold." And he weighed which men to lead down to the shore and which to leave penning the camp.

Meanwhile Aeneas was putting his men ashore — some down gangplanks, some leaping straight off the boats where the tide ran shallow. Tarchon watched the coast with a careful eye, and where he found no surf breaking, no ridge of foam, only the swell sliding smooth up the beach, he turned his ships in and called out: "Now, men — bend to the oars, and drive her aground at any cost. Let the keel cut a furrow in this hateful enemy soil. Once I've landed I don't care if the ship breaks up under me." The men threw themselves on the oars and ran the vessels onto the dry sand, every hull jarring with the shock but holding — all but Tarchon's own, which stuck on a sandbank, hung there pounded by the waves until her back cracked and her timbers split and pitched the Etruscan soldiers into the sea, the broken oars and floating planks tangling around them as they struggled for shore.

Now Turnus led his men down without delay, hard against the water's edge, and the trumpets sounded. Aeneas struck first, into the new-raised farmer-levies, and broke them — and that was the omen of the day. Great Theron fell to him first, a giant of a man who had dared to face the prince head-on: the gilded scales of his armor were no defense, the sword went through his shield and into his bare side. Then Lichas, cut living from his dead mother's womb and dedicated to Apollo because the blade had spared him at birth — but it did not spare him now. Near him Aeneas laid out Cisseus and the huge Gyas, who had been clubbing down whole ranks with the weapons of Hercules; their strength and their famous descent from Alcides' old companion meant nothing. He silenced the bawling Pharos with a thrown spear in mid-shout. He would have killed Cydon too, who chased after Clytius with his soft new beard — except Cydon's seven brothers ringed him round and flung seven spears at once; some glanced off the shield, some rang on the helmet, and the rest his mother Venus turned aside in the air. Then Aeneas called to faithful Achates: "Bring me spears — the ones that drank Greek blood under the walls of Troy. Not one of them will I throw in vain at these Rutulians." He seized a great spear and threw: it tore through Maeon's bronze shield and into his heart, and as his brother Alcanor reached out to hold him up, a second spear pinned that reaching arm and dragged it down dead at his side. Then Numitor wrenched the spear from his dead brother's body and threw it back, but fate turned it aside; it only grazed Achates' thigh.

Now Clausus the Sabine came on in the pride of his youth and took aim at Dryops from a distance: the spear flew hissing and drove through his throat, cutting off voice and breath together, and he pitched forward, the dark blood pouring out with his life. Clausus killed three sons of the north wind's line, and three more whom their country Ismara had sent to war, all of them Thracians. Halesus came up leading the Aurunci, and Messapus, son of Neptune, fought beside him on horseback. On this side and that they struggled — one army to hold the land, the other to take it — and the soil of Italy ran with the blood of both, like two winter winds locked in the sky, equal in their fury, roaring against each other while the clouds hang motionless between them and the sea lies undriven, neither able to give way. So the lines stood, foot against foot, man against man.

But in another part of the field the Arcadian horsemen were faring badly against the Latins. Where a flooding torrent had torn down crags and uprooted trees and left the ground broken, they had left their horses behind — and, unused to fighting on foot, they were scattering in a shameful rout. Pallas saw it: his own men running, the enemy at their backs, and grief and disdain rose in him. He used threats and prayers both, the last thing left to him, to turn their minds and fire their blood. "Where are you running? Where? By your own selves, by the great battles you've won, by my father's name and the early fame I've staked my life to earn — don't shame yourselves with flight. We have to hack our way home through the thick of that black mass of them. That's the only road there is. No power above and no fate below is pressing us; we go with mortal strength to meet a mortal enemy. Look where we stand — a narrow strip of beach, the sea at our backs, the enemy in front, no road left unless we swim. Forward, then, through them, and on to the Trojan camp." And he strode in among the thickest of them.

Lagus was the first he met, dragged there by an unlucky fate — he had stooped to lift a heavy stone, and Pallas drove the spear through the middle of his back, where the spine divides the ribs, and had to wrench the point loose from the bone. Hisbon came at him next, too slow for the revenge he wanted; Pallas met the blow and plunged his sword into the man's wide-open chest. Then he laid lewd Anchemolus in the dust, the man who had defiled his own stepmother's bed. And then the twin sons of Daucus, Larides and Thymber, so alike in face and build that their own parents used to mistake one for the other — a sweet confusion, until the sword settled it cruelly: Thymber's head was lopped off, and Larides' right hand, cut away, went groping after its owner across the ground, the dying fingers still twitching on the hilt. The Arcadians, shamed and stung by the sight of his deeds, rallied and came back into the fight. Then Pallas brought down Rhoeteus as he fled past in his chariot — the spear had been aimed at Ilus, but Rhoeteus crossed its path and took the death meant for another, rolling from his car to spurn the ground in his last spasm.

And as a shepherd in summer, when the wind serves, scatters fire through the heart of a wood, and the flames leap and catch from crown to crown until the whole forest goes up in one roaring blaze and the shepherd sits watching the sheet of fire climb the sky in triumph — so all the courage of Pallas's men gathered into one and poured against the enemy. But Halesus came at them, fierce for blood, and cut down Ladon, Demodocus, and Pheres; he swung his bright sword and sheared off Strymonius's hand, lifted to guard his throat, then crushed Thoas's forehead with a thrown stone so the bone burst and brain and blood flew together. Halesus's father, a seer who had read his son's fate, had hidden the boy away in lonely woods; but when the old man's own life ran out, the Fates laid hold of the son and dragged him to the war, to die under Evander's spear. Pallas met him, but first he prayed to the Tiber: "Holy stream, guide my flying spear and grant it a clear way through proud Halesus's heart. Your oak shall hold his arms and his spoils." The god heard. And while Halesus stood shielding a friend in trouble, the spear came driving on and pierced his unguarded breast.

But Lausus, no small part of that war, would not let panic spread among his men because so famous a fighter had fallen; he steadied the line by his own example. First he killed fierce Abas, the brace and mainstay of the Trojan ranks, the one who had held the day. The men of Troy went down, and their mixed allies with them. Then both armies crashed together, the leaders evenly matched, the strength on each side the same, the rear so packed against the front that no man had room to swing his weapon. Here Pallas pressed forward, there Lausus — two boys, alike in youth and beauty, both forbidden by fate ever to see their homelands again. Yet the king of Olympus would not let them meet hand to hand: each was doomed, but to fall under a greater hand soon enough.

Now the divine sister Juturna warned Turnus that Lausus was in danger, and he wheeled his chariot through the crowd to reach his friends, calling out: "Stand off — leave the field clear. This fight is mine alone. Pallas belongs to me, and to me only. I wish his father were here to watch." His men drew back from the ground he had claimed. Pallas, struck with wonder at the man's haughty command, his towering height and his proud face, ran his eyes over him and answered the king: "Either I'll win the great spoils I'm after, or I'll win a good death — and my father can bear either one. Spare me your threats." And he stepped out into the open space. The blood drained from every Arcadian face. Turnus leapt down from his chariot to fight on foot, on equal terms, and came on like a lion that has spotted a bull far off on the plain, lowering its head to charge, and comes roaring down from its hilltop. That was Turnus, rushing his unequal enemy.

When Pallas judged him near enough for the cast, he threw first — staking everything on courage, since his strength fell short — and he prayed: "By the table you shared and the welcome my father Evander gave you, Hercules, help me now. Let Turnus see me strip his bloody armor with his dying eyes." Hercules heard the boy, and choked back a groan deep in his chest, and wept useless tears. Then Jupiter spoke gently to his son: "Each man has his own short day. The span of life is brief and never given back. But to stretch your fame by what you do — that is the work of courage. Under the high walls of Troy so many sons of gods went down. My own son Sarpedon fell there. Turnus, too, has his fate calling him; he stands already at the edge of his allotted years." So he spoke, and turned his eyes away from the Latin fields. Pallas hurled his spear with all his force and drew his shining sword; the point flew home where the armor joins the shoulder, and forcing through the rim of the shield it even grazed great Turnus's body. Then Turnus, taking long aim with his oak-shafted spear, threw, and said: "See now whose weapon bites the deeper." The iron drove clean through the center of the shield, through all its plates of bronze and bull's-hide layered over each other, through the corselet, and into the great breast. In vain the boy tore the hot spear from the wound — blood and life came out the same way together. He fell forward over the wound, his armor clanging upon him, and bit the enemy ground with his bloody mouth as he died.

Turnus stood over him and said: "Arcadians — carry this word back to Evander: I send him the son he deserved. Whatever honor there is in a tomb, whatever comfort in burial, I grant him freely. His welcome to Aeneas has cost him dear." And with that he set his left foot on the dead boy and tore away the heavy sword-belt, with all its weight of crime worked into the gold: the figures of fifty young men butchered on a single wedding night, the bridal chambers fouled with blood. Eurytion's hand had wrought it. Now Turnus carried it off, glorying in the spoil. Blind, the minds of men, blind to fate and to the lot that is coming, and blind to all restraint when good fortune lifts them up. The day will come when Turnus will give anything to have left Pallas untouched, when he will hate this hour and the plunder he took in it. But for now the Arcadians, weeping, laid their boy on his shield and carried him back off the cruel field — pride and grief of war in one, given back to his father the same day he was sent out, the day that saw him cut down whole heaps of the enemy, and the day that saw him dead and borne home on his shield.

The news reached Aeneas, and not from any vague rumor but from men who had seen it: his friends were on the very edge of ruin, and only his own hand could save the broken Trojans now. Whatever stood in front of him he mowed down with his sword, hacking a wide lane through the enemy in his fury to find Turnus, who was so proud of his fresh kill. Pallas, Evander, the table he had been welcomed at, the hand he had clasped in pledge — all of it stood before his eyes. He took four sons of Sulmo alive and four whom Ufens had raised, taking them living to slaughter as offerings to the shade of Pallas, to be burned in sacrifice at the boy's funeral fire. Then he hurled his spear at Magus — who ducked under it and, as it flew past, came creeping to clasp the hero's knees and beg: "By your father's spirit and by the hope of young Iulus, spare my life for the sake of my own son and my own father. I have a great house, and wealth buried in it — bars of silver, ingots of gold, untold sums no one has counted. The fate of Troy doesn't hang on one life. One soul won't tip the scale." He finished. Aeneas answered him hard: "All your silver and gold — keep it for your children. Turnus tore up the rules of war when he killed Pallas. So judges my father's shade; so judges my living son." And with that, all mercy gone, he gripped the man's helmet, bent his neck back, and drove the sword in to the hilt.

Nearby stood Haemonides, a priest of Apollo and Diana, the sacred fillet bound at his brow, gleaming all over in white robes and bright arms. Aeneas chased him across the field, stood over him where he stumbled and fell, and sent him down into the great shadow; Serestus gathered up his armor to carry off as a trophy for Mars. Then Caeculus, son of Vulcan, and Umbro down from the high hills rallied the Latins again. Against them the Trojan raged on. He sheared off Anxur's left arm with one stroke, shield and all, to the ground — Anxur who had boasted of his magic charms and thought his armor proof against any wound, who had counted on long years secured by spells. Then Tarquitus came strutting up in his bright armor, son of the woodland god Faunus and the nymph Dryope, and dared the prince; Aeneas beat his shield back, pinned his pleading hand, dragged him down, and stood over him while he was still mouthing useless prayers, and cut off his head. He rolled the warm trunk over with his foot and spoke to it: "Lie there now, you fearsome thing. No good mother will bury you; no birds of the air will wait for your bones. You'll be left for the carrion and the fish — or you'll drift to the bottom of the sea, and the hungry monsters will lick your wounds."

He chased down Antaeus and Lucas, Turnus's front-line men, and brave Numa, and golden-haired Camers, son of that Volcens lately killed, the richest man in all the Latin land, who had ruled in quiet over silent Amyclae. Like Aegaeon, the hundred-handed giant who once stood against Jupiter himself — they say he flashed fire from fifty mouths and fifty breasts and clanged on fifty shields and brandished as many swords against the lightning — so Aeneas raged victorious across the whole plain once his blade had tasted blood. He flew at Niphaeus and his four-horse team: the horses, seeing him come on with his spear lowered at their chests, wheeled in terror, threw their master headlong, and bolted with the empty chariot toward the shore. Then Lucagus and Liger drove up with their two white horses, Liger holding the reins, bold Lucagus on the high seat with his sword. Liger shouted: "These aren't Diomedes's horses, this isn't Achilles's chariot, and Venus's veil won't save you here. Your last hour has come on this field." And as Lucagus bent forward to whip the team on, his left foot braced for the fight, the spear came and tore through the lower rim of his shield and into his groin, and pitched him from the car to the ground. Aeneas spoke to him in scorn: "Lucagus, no slow horses lost you the chariot, no shadow on the field turned them back. You jumped off it yourself." And he caught the team by the reins; Liger had already fallen with the same crash, and now he stretched out his hands and begged: "By your own self, by the parents who made you so godlike, spare me — pity a suppliant." Aeneas cut him short: "That isn't the way you talked before. Die — and stay a good brother to your brother." And he sent the sword through his chest, where the soul came out the open wound. So the Trojan stormed across the plain like a flood, like a tearing torrent, scattering death — until at last Ascanius and the Trojan garrison broke out of the camp that had been besieged so long in vain.

Meanwhile Jupiter spoke to Juno of his own accord: "My sister, and my wife — and how rightly so — you were sure Venus's help was holding the Trojans up. But look: see how high their courage runs, how they stand the fight, undaunted. Judge for yourself whether such men need a goddess at their backs." Juno answered him low, her tone all submission: "Why hurt me with this, my lord, when I dread your frown and can't bear your anger lightly? If I still had the power over your will that I once had, you would not deny your wife this much — to lift Turnus out of the battle and give him back safe to his old father's sight. As it is, let him die, then, since it pleases you, and let his pious blood glut the Trojans. And yet he comes of our own line; Pilumnus, four generations back, was his ancestor; and his hand has heaped your altars high with offerings." Jupiter answered briefly: "If all you're asking is a little stay, a short reprieve from death for a man already doomed, and you trust me to grant that much — then take Turnus away in flight, and snatch him from the fate that's bearing down on him. So far I can yield. But if some deeper hope is hiding under your plea, if you think to change the whole course of the war and the fate of it, you are feeding yourself on air." Juno answered, weeping: "What if your heart granted what your tongue refuses, and Turnus were given not a brief reprieve but long, sure life? As it is, a swift death waits for the guiltless boy — or my foreboding fails me. Oh, may I be wrong, frightened of nothing; and you have the power — bend the fates, and lengthen his years."

Having said it, she dropped down out of high heaven wrapped in cloud, driving a storm before her through the sky, and came to earth where the Latins and the Trojans were locked in their doubtful fight. There, out of thin mist, she shaped a phantom — a hollow likeness of Aeneas, an eerie thing — and dressed it in Trojan armor, with the crest and the shield, and gave it the great hero's bearing and an empty voice and a stride that mimicked his. It moved among the lines, daring Turnus, brandishing its sword in the air. Turnus came at it and threw his spear; the phantom wheeled and ran as if in fear. Believing Aeneas had fled, drunk on the false hope of it, Turnus shouted after it: "Where are you going, Aeneas? Don't desert your promised bride! This is the hand that will give you the land you crossed the seas for." And he chased the fleeing shadow, his sword out. A ship happened to lie moored to the shore, the one that had brought King Osinius from old Clusium, the gangplank still down; onto it the trembling phantom fled and hid below the hatches. Turnus, careless in his triumph, ran up the plank and onto the deck — and the moment he reached the prow, Juno cut the cable and shot the ship out to sea on a running wind. Meanwhile the real Aeneas was hunting his absent enemy across the field, sending down to the dead every man he met.

Now the empty phantom no longer sought a hiding place; it rose into the air and melted into a dark cloud, while Turnus was carried far out over the water, still driving away from the land. He looked back, understanding too late how he had been used, and lifted his hands and his wild eyes to heaven, ungrateful for a life saved by such shame: "Almighty Father — did you think me so guilty as to deserve this disgrace? Where am I being taken, and from what? How can I ever go back, and with what reproach? Will I ever see the Latin plain again, or the high towers of Laurentum? What will they say of me — the men I led to slaughter and then abandoned, whose dying groans I can hear even now behind me, while I run? Open, earth, and swallow me down alive! Or you, winds, take pity — drive the ship onto the rocks, onto the shoals, onto some empty shore where no Rutulian can ever find me, where even rumor can't follow." Three times he reached for his sword to fall on it, three times he made to throw himself into the sea — but Juno, in her pity, three times held him back. The ship ran on across the swell on a strong wind, and brought him at last to his native shore and to his father's longing arms.

Meanwhile, by Jupiter's prompting, Mezentius took the field where Turnus had left it, and fell on the victorious Trojans, breathing his own fury into his men. The Etruscan ranks closed on him together — on this one man and no other they spent all their hate, all their longing for revenge, all their spears. He stood like a rock thrust out into the deep, taking the full rage of the winds and the waves head-on, looking down from his height on the menace of the sea, and never moving. He cut down Hebrus, son of Dolichaon, and Latagus, and Palmus fleeing — he flung a great stone at Latagus that smashed his face and helmet, and hamstrung Palmus from behind so he sprawled writhing on the ground, and gave Palmus's crest and armor to his son Lausus to wear. He killed Evanthes the Phrygian, and Mimas, born on the same night Hecuba bore Paris — but Paris died in the fields of Troy, and Mimas, far from home, lay dead on a Latin plain. Like a wild boar bred on the mountains, fattened in the marshes, when the hunters and the baying hounds have ringed it in — it whets its tusks and turns at bay, and they dart their javelins from a safe distance and shout but none dares come close, while the beast froths and bristles and shakes the spears from its flanks — so the men whetted by their hatred of the tyrant kept up the fight only from a distance, clamoring and hurling, and none dared close with him.

From Corythus came Acron to the war, a Greek who had left his betrothed and the wedding night unconsummated; Mezentius saw him riding through the ranks, bright in the crimson favors his bride had given him, and rushed him like a starved lion that has spotted a frisking goat or a tall stag and runs, roaring, mane rising, jaws gaping wide — and the prey lies pinned and panting under the bloody paws, the lion's mouth running over with gore. So Mezentius hurled himself on his enemies, and Acron went down first, stretched full-length on the dark ground, the broken spear lying red in the wound. But Mezentius scorned to strike Orodes in the back as he fled, or to win him by a thrown spear; he ran round, met him face to face, and beat him in fair fight, the better man not by stealth but by strength. Then he set his foot on the fallen body, leaned on his spear, and cried: "Here lies Orodes — no small part of the war." His men took it up with a shout of triumph. But Orodes gasped out with his dying breath: "You won't go long unpunished, whoever you are. The same death is waiting for you on this same field." Mezentius answered with a grim half-smile: "What concerns me, let the Father of gods and king of men see to. Die now." And he drew the weapon from the wound. A heavy mist came swimming over Orodes' eyes and sealed them in everlasting night.

Caedicus killed Alcathous, Sacrator killed Hydaspes, Rapo brought down Parthenius and the mighty Orses; Messapus killed Clonius and the Lycian Ericetes — Clonius thrown from his bolting horse and pinned on the ground, Ericetes met on foot. Agis of Lycia stepped out to challenge the boldest, but Valerus, no shame to his father's prowess, cut him down. Salius killed Thronius; Nealces killed Salius — Nealces, deadly with the spear and with the far-reaching arrow that strikes before it's seen. So death was traded for death, grief for grief, between them; by turns they gave ground and gained it, killers and killed alike, neither side wholly winning, neither wholly broken. And the gods in Jupiter's halls looked down and pitied the useless rage of both, and grieved that mortals had to bear such suffering — Venus on one side watching, Saturnian Juno on the other; and pale Tisiphone raged in the thick of the thousands.

But now Mezentius, brandishing his great spear, stormed into the middle of the plain — towering there in the center like giant Orion wading the deep, his head above the topmost waves where he cuts a path through the water on foot, or like an old mountain ash, its head hidden in the clouds, its roots driven deep. Aeneas saw him from far off and came on to meet him. Mezentius held his ground unmoved, a mass waiting for its enemy; he measured with his eye the throw of the spear and cried: "My right hand, and the spear I'm balancing now — be my gods. I make no other vow. I'll dress you, Lausus, in the armor I strip from this Trojan pirate's body; you'll be the trophy of Aeneas." And he threw with all his force; the spear flew hissing, glanced off Aeneas's shield, and drove on at an angle into the body of Antores nearby — Antores, the companion of Hercules, who had come from Argos and stayed in Italy at Evander's side; now he fell by a wound meant for another, and looked up at the sky, and thought of Argos far away as he died.

Then dutiful Aeneas threw his spear in turn. It went through the hollow shield's three layers of bronze, through the linen and the three bull-hides, and lodged in Mezentius's groin, but the force was spent. Glad at the sight of the man's blood, Aeneas drew his sword and pressed in hard on his shaken enemy. And Lausus, seeing it, groaned aloud for love of his father, and the tears ran down his face. Here, brave boy, I will not be silent about your death, nor about your deed — so noble, so hard to believe, that men to come may doubt it. Mezentius, crippled by the wound and dragging the enemy spear that hung in his shield, gave ground and tried to pull back out of the fight. His son sprang forward into the middle of it. Just as Aeneas rose with his sword lifted to strike, Lausus came up under the blade and took it on his own shield and held the blow, while his father slipped away behind him, alive. His comrades roared and rained their spears to drive the Trojan off, and Aeneas, furious, sheltered under the cover of his shield — like a farmer caught in a hailstorm who huddles in any hollow until the sky clears.

But Aeneas kept calling out a warning even then, in anger and in pity both: "Why are you rushing on a death you can't survive? Why dare more than your strength can bear? Your love for your father is making a fool of you." Still the boy would not stop, pressing on, taunting; and the prince's patience gave way at last, and his whole chest filled with rage. The Fates were already gathering up the last threads of Lausus's life. Aeneas drove his strong sword full into the boy, to the hilt — through the light shield, the soft armor, the tunic his mother had woven him with gold thread — and filled his breast with blood. The soul went out of him sorrowing through the air, down to the shades, and left the body behind. But when Aeneas, son of Anchises, looked at the dying boy's face, that face going strangely pale, he groaned in deep pity and stretched out his hand, and the thought of his own love for his own father went through him. "Poor boy — what can dutiful Aeneas give you that's worthy of such courage, such a heart? Keep the armor you were so glad of; and I give your body back to your own people, your own dead, to be buried as you'd want. And let this be a comfort, if comfort there is: you fell by the hand of great Aeneas." And he lifted the body up himself, the hair clotted with blood, and called the boy's hanging-back companions to come and take it.

Meanwhile his father stood by the Tiber's tawny stream, washing his wounds in the water, his weary body propped against a tree-trunk, his bronze helmet hung on a branch overhead, his heavy arms laid out on the grass. The chosen young men stood around him while he leaned his sick, heavy head on his hand, his beard spilling over his chest, asking again and again for word of Lausus, sending messenger after messenger to call the boy back out of the fight — in his father's name, to come away. But they were already carrying Lausus, dead, weeping over him on his shield, a great body brought down by a great wound. The father's mind read the sound of their grief from far off, before they came. He fouled his gray hair with dust, lifted both hands to heaven, and threw himself on the body. "My son — was I so in love with living that I let you stand in my place against the enemy's sword, your wounds for mine? Am I saved by your death? Is this exile of mine only now, at last, truly bitter — the wound now driven home? It was I, my son, who stained your name with my crimes, I who got myself driven from my throne and my fathers' kingdom by the hate I earned. I owed my country that punishment; I should have paid it with my own guilty life a hundred deaths over. And yet I'm still alive — I haven't yet left the light and the company of men. But I will leave it."

And with that he raised himself on his crippled thigh, and though the deep wound slowed him he did not flinch; he called for his horse — Rhaebus, his pride and his comfort, that had carried him out of every battle — and spoke to him with sorrow: "Rhaebus, we've lived a long time, if anything for mortals lasts long. Today you'll either carry back the bloody head and the spoils of Aeneas and avenge Lausus's death with me, or, if no road opens that way, you'll go down with me. For I don't think, brave one, you'd ever take a foreign master's orders, or a Trojan rider." Then he mounted, settling his weight onto the horse's back as he'd always done, and loaded both hands with sharp javelins, his bronze helmet on his head, bright with its tossing horsehair crest, and drove headlong into the thick of the fight. In his heart at once a great wave of shame, of madness, of grief, of love mixed with fury, and the knowledge of his own worth.

Three times he shouted Aeneas by name, in a great voice. Aeneas knew it, and rejoiced, and prayed: "So may the Father of the high gods grant it, and Apollo — come, begin." That was all he said, and he advanced with his spear leveled. Mezentius answered: "Why try to frighten me, you cruel man, now that you've taken my son? That was the one way you could destroy me. I don't fear death, and I spared none of your gods. Enough — I come to die, but first take these gifts from me." And he hurled a javelin, then another, and another, wheeling in a wide ring around his enemy; but the golden shield held. Three times he rode his circle round Aeneas, throwing as he went, and three times the Trojan turned with him, carrying a whole forest of spears in his shield. At last, weary of pulling out dart after dart and of fighting always on the defensive, hard-pressed and unequally matched, Aeneas made up his mind: he flung his spear straight between the temples of the war-horse. The animal reared up, lashing the air with its hooves, threw its rider, and came down on top of him in a tangle, pinning his shoulder under its weight, its own forequarters dislocated.

Trojans and Latins both filled the sky with their shouting. Aeneas ran up, drew his sword, and stood over him: "Where is fierce Mezentius now, and that wild spirit of yours?" The Etruscan, staring up at the sky, gathering back his senses, answered: "Why taunt me, enemy, why throw death in my face? There's no shame in my dying; I didn't come to the field expecting to live, and my son struck no bargain with you for my life. I ask one thing only — if a beaten enemy may ask any mercy: let my body be covered with earth. I know how my own people's hatred surrounds me. Keep their fury off me, I beg you, and let me share my son's grave." He said it, and offered his throat to the sword, knowing what was coming, and poured his life out over his armor in a flood of blood.

sections.label: Book XI
sections.title: The Death of Pallas, the Council, and Camilla

segments.text: Dawn rose meanwhile out of the sea and left the ocean behind her. Aeneas, though grief pressed him hard, gave the morning to his vows — there was the burying of his dead, and his mind was a wreck with sorrow, but a victor pays the gods first. So on a rising mound he set a great oak with its boughs lopped clean away, and dressed the bare trunk in the gleaming arms he had stripped from the captain Mezentius: a trophy to you, mighty Lord of War. He fixed the plumed crest on it, still wet with blood, the broken spears, the breastplate punched through and dented in twelve places; he bound the bronze shield to the left and hung the ivory-hilted sword from its neck. Then, ringed by his officers — for they all crowded close — he gave them their triumph in words:

“The hardest of it is done, men. Let go your fear of what’s left. These are the spoils — the first-fruits taken from a proud king, and Mezentius, by my own hand, is what you see here. Now the road runs to the king and the walls of the Latins. Get your weapons ready; lift up your hearts; look for the war so that the moment Heaven gives the word no one is caught unready, no one fumbling, no one pleading he didn’t know. But first — while the gods above let us — let’s lay our unburied comrades in the earth. That is the one honor that still means anything down in Acheron. Go,” he said, “give these brave souls their last rites, the men whose blood bought us this country. And before anything else, send Pallas home to the grieving city of Evander — Pallas, who lacked no courage, and whom a black day stole away and drowned in bitter death.”

So he spoke, weeping, and turned back to the doorway where the body of Pallas lay. Old Acoetes was keeping watch over it — once squire to Evander in Arcadia, now sent out under far worse stars to attend the son. Around them stood the whole household of the dead boy, the Trojan ranks, the Trojan women with their hair torn loose in mourning. When Aeneas came through the high doors they lifted a great cry to heaven and beat their breasts, and the palace rang with the sound of grief. But when he saw the pale face and the open wound — the spear-gash high in that smooth young chest, made by an Ausonian point — he could not hold back the tears, and he said:

“Poor boy. Did Fortune, when she came at last in all her brightness, begrudge me only this — that you should never see my kingdom, never ride home beside me in triumph? This is not the promise I made your father the day I rode away. He threw his arms around me and sent me off to win a great command, and warned me, frightened, that the men I faced were fierce, that I was going to war with a hard people. And right now, maybe, fooled by an empty hope, he is heaping his altars high with offerings and prayers — while we walk back to him in this useless funeral pomp, owing nothing more to anyone but the powers below, and carry him his son, a dead thing that can pay no other debt. The poor father will see the burial of his own boy before his own life is run. These are my triumphs in the Latin war. This is what my given word was worth, and all my care. And yet, Evander — you will not look on a son shamed by some wound in the back. You will not have to wish, too late, that you’d died yourself rather than live to see him. Italy, what a champion you have lost. Ascanius — what a friend.”

When he had finished mourning he gave the order to lift the wretched body and chose a thousand men, the flower of the whole army, to walk in the funeral train, to share Evander’s tears and carry the boy home — a small comfort for so great a grief, but the most they could give. They wove a soft bier out of oak shoots and arbutus and shaded it over with green leaves, and on this rough country litter they laid the boy on his high bed. He looked like a flower a girl’s fingers have cut from the stem — a soft violet, a hyacinth letting go its head — the sheen and the shape of it still there, not yet faded; but the earth that mothered it no longer feeds it, no longer gives it strength.

Then Aeneas brought out two robes stiff with gold and purple, which Sidonian Dido had once made for him with her own hands, glad in the work, threading the gold through the weave herself. One of these he wrapped around the boy, a last honor; in the other he covered the hair that the fire would soon take. He piled up beside the bier the spoils of the men Pallas had killed in the Latin fighting, and ordered his trophies carried out in a long line — the captured horses, the captured arms. He brought out the men too, hands bound behind them, to be sent down as offerings to the dead, their blood meant to sprinkle the flames. And he had the officers carry tree-trunks dressed in enemy armor with the names of the conquered fixed to them. Acoetes was led along, broken with age, bruising his breast with his fists, raking his old face with his nails, and again and again throwing himself full-length on the ground. They led out the war-chariots too, splashed with Rutulian blood. Behind came the war-horse, Aethon, his harness stripped off, weeping — yes, weeping, great drops wetting his face. Others carried Pallas’s spear and helmet; the rest of his gear Turnus had taken. After came the whole grieving column — Trojans, Etruscans, the Arcadians with their weapons reversed and trailing in the dust. When the long procession had wound far ahead, Aeneas stopped and gave a last groan: “The same grim war that calls us calls me away from these other tears. Goodbye forever, great Pallas. Goodbye.” He said no more, but turned for the walls and went back to camp.

And now men came from the Latin city carrying olive branches, asking for mercy: would he give back the bodies that lay strewn over the field, let them bury their dead? No one makes war on men with no breath left in them, they said; spare those who only yesterday were his hosts, the kin of the bride he had been promised. Aeneas, who could not refuse so fair a thing, granted it, and said more besides: “Latins — what cruel turn of luck has tangled you in a war like this and set you against a man who is your friend? You ask me for peace for your dead, for men cut down by the lot of war. I’d gladly give it to your living too. I never came here except that the fates assigned me this place to settle. I make no war on your people. It was your king who broke off our bond and chose to trust himself to Turnus instead. It would have been fairer for Turnus to face this death himself. If he means to end the war by his own hand, if he means to drive the Trojans out, this is where he should have come and crossed weapons with me — and let the one live to whom the god or his own right arm gives the day. Now go, and light the fires under your poor dead.” He finished. They stood stunned, silent, looking at one another.

Then Drances — an older man, who had long carried a grudge against young Turnus and never hid his hate — broke the silence and answered: “Trojan, great in your fame and greater in your arms — how can I raise you to the heaven you deserve? Should I admire your justice first, or your strength in war? We’ll carry your words home gratefully, and if luck lets us in any way, we’ll join you to Latinus our king. Let Turnus go find his own alliances. We’ll even be glad to set the stones of the city the fates have promised you, and carry the Trojan walls on our backs.” So Drances said, and all of them murmured the same. They struck a truce of twelve days, and in that peace Latins and Trojans wandered the wooded hills together, harming no one, and felled the timber for the pyres. The axes rang through the groves; they brought down the high ash trees, split the oak and the sweet-smelling cedar with wedges, and hauled the loads away on groaning wagons.

And now Rumor — who only days before had carried news of Pallas’s triumphs ahead of him — flew through the little Arcadian town with word of his death, and filled Evander’s ears, and his house, and his streets. The people poured out of the gates with funeral torches in their hands, and the long line of fire lit up the fields and threw a sullen glare over the marching column and the dead prince at the heart of it. When the two crowds met, the wail went up, and the women answered it from the walls, and the whole town shook with the cry. Nothing could keep Evander back. He came stumbling out into the middle of it all, threw himself down on the bier where they had set Pallas, and held on, weeping and groaning, until at last grief forced a path for his voice:

“This is not the promise you gave your father, Pallas — that you’d be careful, that you’d not throw yourself into the savage god of war. I knew too well how much a young man’s first taste of glory can carry him away, how sweet that honor is in a first battle. Bitter first-fruits of your soldiering, hard lesson in a war fought so close to home, and not one of my vows heard, not one of my prayers answered. And you, my dear wife, lucky in your death — you went before this grief could find you. I have lived past my own time, outlasted my own fate, just to be left standing here, a father who has buried his son. If only I had ridden with the Trojans and gone down myself under the Rutulian spears — then this funeral would be bringing me home, not Pallas. And yet I won’t blame the Trojans, won’t curse the bond we made; this loss is the lot old age was always owed. But if an early death was waiting for my boy, at least let it comfort me that he fell leading the way into Latium, with Volscians cut down in heaps before he died. Pallas, I could wish you no better funeral than the one dutiful Aeneas has given you, than the Trojans and the great Etruscan chiefs and all their host. They carry the trophies of the men your own hand killed. You too, Turnus, would be standing here now, a great trunk hung with armor, if Pallas had matched you in years and strength. But why do I hold the Trojans here, miserable as I am? Go — take this message to your king. The one reason I drag out a life I hate, now that my son is dead, is your right hand: you owe me Turnus, owe him to the son and the father both, and you know it. This is the one thing left for your courage and your luck to give. I ask no joy in this life — there is none — only to carry the news to my Pallas, down among the shades.”

Dawn meanwhile had lifted her kindly light again and brought work and grief back with it. Now Aeneas and Tarchon raised the pyres along the curving shore. Each man carried his own dead there by the old custom, and as the fires were kindled the black smoke smothered the high air and blotted out the sky. Three times in their gleaming armor they rode around the burning piles; three times on foot they circled the flames, crying out the names of the dead; and the tears ran down their cheeks and wet the ground. Trumpets and shields rang into the sound of weeping. Some threw onto the fire the spoils stripped from the slain Latins — helmets, fine swords, bridles, the hot chariot-wheels; some cast in offerings each man knew, the very shields and unlucky spears those friends had carried. All around, oxen were slaughtered to the fire, and bristle-backed boars, and sheep gathered from the fields, killed and laid in the flames. Along the whole shore they watched their comrades burn and would not leave the smoldering pyres until damp night wheeled the sky over, set thick with burning stars.

Elsewhere the wretched Latins built their own countless pyres. Many of their dead they buried where they fell; many they carried off to the neighboring fields or home to the city. The rest — a vast tangled heap, beyond counting and beyond names — they burned together unhonored, and the fields were thick with fires on every side. When the third dawn had driven the cold shadows from the sky, the men still keeping the pyres raked the deep ash, sifted out the white bones, gathered them while they were warm, and heaped a mound of earth over them. But in the city, in the king’s own house, the grief ran deepest and longest — mothers, brides, the loving hearts of sisters, orphaned boys all cursing the war and Turnus’s marriage. Let the man fight it out himself, they said; let the one who claims the crown of Italy, who wants to be king, settle it hand to hand. Drances fed the fire, swearing Aeneas wanted no one but Turnus, called only for Turnus. But Turnus had his own party too, and plenty of them; the queen’s great name covered him like a shield, and the trophies of his old victories held his fame up.

Into all this heat the envoys came back from Diomedes — the great Greek hero who had built a new city in Italy. They came with the worst possible news: nothing had come of all the cost and the long road; their gifts had moved him not at all, their prayers not at all; the Latins would have to look elsewhere for an ally, or buy peace from the Trojan king. Latinus, sunk in grief, saw now too late that the fates plainly pointed to a foreign son-in-law, an outsider Heaven itself was bringing in — and that until Aeneas married Lavinia, divine anger would hang over the land. The gods had backed the better cause; the fresh graves and the undried tears all said so. So, full of dread, he called the whole Latin council to the great hall. The chiefs came at his summons and crowded the road to the palace. Latinus, oldest of them and first in power, took the throne in their midst, the weight of the day in his face, and told Venulus to report.

At once the murmuring died and a hush fell, and Venulus began: “We did as you ordered, citizens — crossed a long stretch of dangerous country and reached the place. We saw with our own eyes the Greek camp, the rising towers. Diomedes has walled in the city he calls Argyripa, named for his own Argos. We were brought in; we set our gifts before him; we gave our names and our country and told him plainly why we’d come. He listened to it all, and then answered us, gently and without anger: ‘You old race of Ausonia, you children of Saturn’s golden peace — what madness has come over you, to give up your ancient calm and stir up a war you don’t understand, to lay hands on the sword? Every one of us who put steel into the fields of Ilium — set aside the men killed in the fighting, or swallowed by the Simois — every one of us has paid for it across the whole world, in suffering no king would wish on Priam himself. Minerva’s storm knows it, and the rocks of Caphereus, and the avenging coast of Euboea. Menelaus, who led us, was driven all the way to Egypt; Ulysses saw the Cyclops’ cave. Why even name Idomeneus, thrown out of his own kingdom — or Agamemnon, the lord of all the Greeks, the man who avenged a stolen wife, cut down on his own threshold by an adulterous wife of his own, the moment he came home? As for me — the gods grudged me ever seeing my own country again, my own dear wife. Even now strange portents follow me: my lost companions turned to birds and gone up into the air, and they haunt the rivers — God, the cruelty of it — and fill the cliffs with their crying. I should have known what was coming, the day I was mad enough to lift a mortal hand against the gods, and wounded Venus herself. No. Don’t push me into wars like that again. I have no quarrel left with Troy now that her towers are down; I take no joy in the old wrongs. The gifts you’ve brought me from home — give them to Aeneas instead. I have stood against his spear, fought him hand to hand: believe a man who knows, how he rises behind his shield, the whirlwind he throws a spear with. If the land of Ida had bred two more like him, the Trojans would be the ones besieging Greek cities now, and Greece would be in mourning. Whatever held us up so long under the walls of Troy — what blunted the Greek victory and dragged the war out ten years — it was the hands of those two, Hector and Aeneas; both of them brave past telling, both first in war, but Aeneas first of all in duty to the gods. Whatever terms he offers, take his right hand. Just be careful your weapons never cross with his.’ That, my king, is his answer, and his counsel on this great war.” So Venulus closed his report.

A jarring murmur ran through the troubled council, the way water roars when a current jams between rocks, and the river, hemmed into a narrow channel, churns and rebounds and the banks throw the sound back. When the noise died down, Latinus called on the gods and spoke from his high throne: “I wish, Latins, we had settled this before — and not be holding a council now, with the enemy camped at the walls. We are fighting a hopeless war, citizens, against men who can’t be beaten in the field and won’t put down their swords even when they are. Whatever hope you pinned on Diomedes, let it go. You’ve seen for yourselves how thin our own hope is, how near ruin we are. I don’t blame anyone — every man fought with all his strength, and we threw the whole weight of the kingdom into it. So now hear what I think. There’s an old tract of land of mine along the Tuscan river, running far to the west, past the old Sicanian borders; Rutulians and Auruncans sow it now and graze the rough hills. Let us give that whole upland, and the pine-covered ridge, to the Trojans — make them partners in our country on fair terms, and invite them to settle there. Or if they’d rather build elsewhere and leave our soil, let us cut them twenty ships of Italian oak, or more if they can man them; the timber’s down by the water’s edge — let them name the number and the shape, and the bronze and the labor and the shipyards are mine to give. And to carry the terms, let a hundred of our noblest go, olive in hand, with gifts — gold, a robe of state, the ivory chair and the kingly crown. Talk it over among yourselves, and save a kingdom that is sinking.”

Then Drances rose — the man who had hated the bright young Turnus for years. He was rich, a power at the council table, and a fine speaker; but in the field his hand went cold. He was a born plotter, brave with his tongue. Highborn through his mother, his father he never named. He stood up and laid it on thick: “You’ve said it all, great king, and said it so plainly there’s no arguing — and there’s not a man here who doesn’t see what the country needs. They just don’t dare to say it. Let him give us leave to speak — that arrogant man whose pride and whose luck started this miserable war. I’ll say it though it costs me my life. Because of him the plains of Latium run with blood; because of his ambition our best men lie in the dirt; the whole town is in mourning, the whole land in tears. And he, the cause of all of it, the man who keeps threatening the gods with his arms — when it came to the worst he ran, and looked to his own safety in a shameful flight. Best of kings, since you’re sending all these rich gifts to the Trojan, add one more, the one he wants above the rest, and let no man’s bullying stop you: give Aeneas your daughter Lavinia for his wife. Seal the bond with that marriage and give this bleeding land a lasting peace. And Turnus — I know you count me no friend, and I won’t fight you on that. I’ll only beg you: pity your people, lay down your pride, and step aside, beaten as you are. We’ve buried enough of our own. If it’s glory you want, if you’re that hungry for the throne and the bride, then have the courage to face the man yourself. So that Turnus can win a king’s daughter, are the rest of us — cheap, nameless, unwept — to keep falling in the field? Go, then. If there’s any fight in you, any of your fathers’ courage left, look the man in the eye who’s calling you out.”

Turnus’s fury blazed at this. He groaned from deep in his chest and threw the words back: “Drances, you always have plenty to say, and it’s always when the war needs hands, not voices. First in the council hall, you fill it up with talk — brave words, while the ramparts keep the enemy off and the ditches aren’t yet brimming with blood. So thunder away, eloquent as ever; brand me a coward — you, Drances, whose own hand has piled the field so high with Trojan dead, whose trophies stand so tall! There’s the open country; the foe isn’t far to seek. Shall we go meet them, the two of us? Come on, why wait? Or does the war-god live only in that windy tongue of yours, and your feet, so quick to run? Me, beaten? Me, driven off the field? Who could call that a lie to my face and not be the lowest coward alive — with the Tiber swollen by Trojan blood, with Evander’s whole house cut down root and branch, and the giant brothers stripped of their arms? That’s not how the Trojans found me the day I was fenced inside their walls, alone, one man against the lot of them. A destructive war? Then go threaten the Phrygian pirate with it, and yourself. Keep on filling the people’s ears with your terrors, keep glorifying a race twice beaten, keep running down the arms of Latinus. So the Greek princes tremble before the Trojans now — Diomedes, Achilles, all of them. The river Aufidus runs backward in fear of the Adriatic. The man’s a fraud, and his pretended dread of crossing me is the same fraud — don’t waste your shaking on it, Drances; a soul like yours isn’t worth this hand. Keep it. Let it sit safe in that breast of yours.

“Now, royal father, to you and to the real matter of this council. If you’ve already given up on our arms, if one defeat has us so low we’ll never face the field again, if our luck has turned for good and can’t turn back — then let’s sue for peace, hold out our empty hands and beg. And yet — if there were any of our old courage left in us — to me the man who fell rather than see this, who bit the ground rather than live it, he is the one I’d call blessed beyond the rest. But we still have men in reserve, we still have allies, cities and peoples of Italy ready to bleed for us — and the Trojans paid plenty for what little glory they bought; they have their dead too, and the same storm of war went over them. So why do we throw down our courage at the very door, why does the trembling take us before the trumpet sounds? Time changes many things for the better; Fortune has come and gone and come back to mock men and set them on solid ground again.
